docs.title: graphtrace
docs.text:
Regression testing for LangGraph agents, built as a pytest plugin.

Status: v0.1 complete, heading toward release

Everything described on this page is real and tested today — 222 tests pass, full regression. See Roadmap & status for the exact build history, including every real bug found and fixed along the way.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Most LangGraph agents are tested the way nothing else in a codebase is: by rereading the final message, or not at all. A graph with branches, retries, and tool calls can look fine on a lucky run while silently changing how it got there — a different node path, a retry that's now happening every time, a tool call that quietly stopped firing, a human-approval gate the agent learned to route around. A test that only checks the final answer text can't catch any of that, because the final answer can still look right while the path that produced it is wrong, expensive, or unsafe.

docs.title: What graphtrace does
docs.text:
graphtrace records a full trajectory of a graph run — every node visited, every state change, every tool and LLM call, in order — and lets a test assert on what the agent did, not just what it said:

assert_path(traj, ["router", ..., "refund"])
assert_tool_called(traj, "refund_api", args_match={"order_id": "1234"})
assert_budget(traj, cost_usd=0.05, latency_s=8)

flowchart LR
    A[pytest test] -->|run_graph| B[Your compiled LangGraph]
    B --> C[Trajectory: path, state, tool/LLM calls]
    C --> D[assert_* functions]
    B -.->|record / replay| E[(Cassettes on disk)]
    C --> F[graphtrace calibrate: judge verdicts]
    C --> G[graphtrace report: HTML + CI]

In replay mode (the intended default for CI), the LLM and tool boxes are never reached — responses come from cassettes, so a test suite runs offline and deterministically. A production trace export (Langfuse/OTel/LangSmith) can also become a cassette + generated test directly, via graphtrace from-trace, without a real LangGraph run at all.

docs.title: Who this is for
docs.text:
• Teams shipping a LangGraph agent to production who want the same regression-testing discipline they'd expect for any other code path, not spot-checks by hand.
  • Anyone refactoring a graph's branching or retry logic who wants a test that fails the moment the path changes, even when the final answer still happens to look right.
  • Consultants and auditors who need a framework-agnostic way to pin down exactly what an agent does before recommending a fix.

docs.title: Design principles that shape every feature
docs.text:
• Framework-agnostic core. Everything downstream of recording — assertions, budgets, the HTML report — works on a plain Trajectory object with no LangGraph import anywhere near it. LangGraph-specific code lives in exactly one layer (frameworks/langgraph/); CrewAI/AutoGen (v0.4) plug into the same core without touching the rest.
  • Offline by default, once cassettes exist. A CI run shouldn't have to call a real model or a real tool to pass.
  • No invented numbers. Cost, token, and judge-agreement figures come from real recorded usage or a real live call, never an estimate.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Requirements: Python 3.10 or newer.

pip install graphtrace

That's it for normal use — graphtrace is on PyPI (v0.1.0, published 2026-10-27) with no extras required: langgraph, langchain-core, ruamel.yaml, pydantic, litellm, scikit-learn, jinja2, and typer all come along as core dependencies. This also registers graphtrace as a pytest plugin automatically (no -p flag needed) and installs a graphtrace console command — confirmed working this way from the real published wheel in a clean, isolated virtualenv, not just an editable dev install.

graphtrace --help

Should show three real commands: from-trace, calibrate, report — see the CLI reference.

docs.title: Install from source (for contributing to graphtrace itself)
docs.text:
This is what the project itself uses for development — needed if you're contributing to graphtrace, not just using it to test your own LangGraph agent.

git clone https://github.com/devbyanoop/graphtrace.git
cd graphtrace
python -m venv .venv
# macOS/Linux:
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows (Git Bash):
source .venv/Scripts/activate

pip install -e ".[dev]"
  • python -m venv .venv creates an isolated Python environment just for this project.
  • -e installs in editable mode — changes under src/graphtrace/ take effect immediately, without reinstalling.
  • [dev] pulls in pytest, python-dotenv, and two real, pinned external apps (langgraph-swarm, deepagents) kept as permanent compatibility tests — not graphtrace's own dependency, gated with pytest.importorskip (see Case study). pyproject.toml's own core dependencies (not an extra) bring in langgraph, langchain-core, ruamel.yaml, pydantic, litellm, scikit-learn, jinja2, and typer — everything the full feature set below needs, installed by default.

Verify the install:

pytest

222 tests should pass, full regression, in well under a minute. Four of those (tests/test_judge_live.py) make a real call to a live Groq model and are skipped cleanly if GROQ_API_KEY isn't set (see .env.example) — everything else runs offline against fake chat models and hand-built fixtures.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
Extra Pulls in Status dev pytest, python-dotenv, langgraph-swarm, deepagents ✅ Available docs mkdocs, mkdocs-material ✅ Available

deepagents itself requires Python ≥3.11 (graphtrace's own floor stays ≥3.10) — it's environment-marked in pyproject.toml so pip install -e ".[dev]" on Python 3.10 simply skips it, and the real compat tests that need it skip cleanly via pytest.importorskip rather than failing the install.

Everything else (langgraph, litellm, pydantic, ruamel.yaml, scikit-learn, jinja2, typer) is a core dependency, installed by default — not behind an extra.

See Roadmap & status for the full build history.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Every example below is real and verified

This walks through a real run_graph() call against examples/refund_agent, the project's own demo agent, then the real graphtrace CLI against a real trace fixture. Run from a cloned checkout (git clone https://github.com/devbyanoop/graphtrace.git) — the commands below assume the repo root as your working directory.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text: Follow Installation first.

docs.title: 2. Run the demo agent
docs.text:
examples/refund_agent is a small, real, compiled LangGraph matching the architecture plan's own running example: router -> lookup_order -> human_approval -> refund. It uses LangChain's own fake chat model, so this needs no API key and makes no real network call.

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "examples")  # repo root; lets this import examples/refund_agent

import itertools
from langchain_core.language_models.fake_chat_models import GenericFakeChatModel
from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage
from refund_agent.graph import build_refund_graph

from graphtrace import run_graph

model = GenericFakeChatModel(messages=itertools.repeat(AIMessage(content="ok")))
graph = build_refund_graph(model)

# resume=[True] supplies the human-in-the-loop approval the graph pauses for --
# see step 5 below for what happens if you leave it out.
traj = run_graph(graph, {"order_id": "1234"}, cassette="tests/cassettes/quickstart.yaml", mode="record", resume=[True])
print(traj.path)           # ['router', 'lookup_order', 'human_approval', 'refund']
print(traj.final_state)    # {..., 'approved': True, 'refunded': True}

docs.title: 3. Replay it with zero real calls
docs.text:
Run it again with mode="replay" instead of "record" — the exact same assert_* calls below pass, but the fake chat model and the get_order tool are never actually invoked; every response comes straight from tests/cassettes/quickstart.yaml. This is what makes CI fast, free, and deterministic once a cassette exists — see Recording & replay.

traj = run_graph(graph, {"order_id": "1234"}, cassette="tests/cassettes/quickstart.yaml", mode="replay", resume=[True])

docs.title: 4. Assert on it
docs.text:
from graphtrace import assert_path, assert_tool_called, assert_budget

assert_path(traj, ["router", "lookup_order", "human_approval", "refund"])
assert_tool_called(traj, "get_order", args_match={"order_id": "1234"})
assert_budget(traj, latency_s=5)

All three pass against the real trajectory above. Change "1234" to "9999" in the second assertion and it raises TrajectoryAssertionError with a readable message telling you which call's args didn't match — try it.

docs.title: 5. What happens without resume
docs.text:
traj = run_graph(graph, {"order_id": "1234"}, cassette="tests/cassettes/quickstart.yaml", mode="live")  # no resume given

from graphtrace import assert_interrupted_at
assert_interrupted_at(traj, "human_approval")
assert traj.interrupted is True
assert "refund" not in traj.path  # the graph paused before ever reaching it

The graph genuinely pauses at human_approval (a real LangGraph interrupt()), and run_graph returns with interrupted=True instead of guessing an answer or hanging.

docs.title: 6. Build a Trajectory by hand instead
docs.text: You don't need a real graph to use the assertion API at all — a Trajectory is just a list of Steps plus a final state. See Core concepts for the shape, or tests/test_assertions.py for a worked example used throughout this project's own test suite.

docs.title: 7. The CLI: turn a production trace into a test
docs.text:
No real LangGraph run needed for this part — graphtrace from-trace converts an exported trace (Langfuse/OTel/LangSmith) straight into a cassette plus a generated pytest file:

graphtrace from-trace my_export.json --target my_app.graph:build_graph

Writes tests/cassettes/from_my_export.yaml and tests/test_from_my_export.py — the generated file replays the observed run and asserts every node that made a captured call was visited, with a # TODO: assert the correct behaviour marker for you to tighten by hand. See Trace-to-test for the real, honest limits (a node with no LLM/tool call is invisible to any trace importer, so the generated assertion is deliberately looser than assert_path).

docs.title: 8. The CLI: grade real outputs with a judge
docs.text:
graphtrace calibrate --rubric refund_reply

Scores a litellm-backed judge against a human-labelled calibration set, reporting agreement % and Cohen's kappa per criterion — see Judge & calibration.

docs.title: 9. The CLI: a static HTML report
docs.text:
pytest --gt-mode=replay --gt-report=reports/graphtrace.html

Every test's trajectory, judge verdicts, and cost/latency totals in one page, no server — see Report & CI.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text:
• Full Assertions reference for every assert_* function, including ones not shown above.
  • Configuration for graphtrace.yaml — the cassette directory, budgets, judge model, and report path all come from there once a project wants to stop repeating them per test.

docs.title: Assertions
docs.text:
All 12 functions below are implemented and tested — src/graphtrace/core/assertions.py, 37 tests in tests/test_assertions.py and tests/test_trajectory.py. Every assertion raises TrajectoryAssertionError (a subclass of AssertionError, so pytest.raises(AssertionError) catches it too) with a message built to be read, not just a repr of two values.

from graphtrace import (
    assert_path, assert_visited, assert_not_visited, assert_visits,
    assert_state, assert_state_at, assert_tool_called, assert_tool_not_called,
    assert_tool_calls_match, assert_retries, assert_interrupted_at,
    assert_budget, any_str,
)

docs.title: assert_path
docs.text:
assert_path(traj, ["router", "lookup_order", "human_approval", "refund"])
assert_path(traj, ["router", ..., "refund"])  # ... = anything in between

Checks the exact sequence of node names visited. Put the literal ... (Python's Ellipsis) at one point to mean "anything can happen here" — useful when a retry loop or a branch makes the middle of a path unpredictable but the start and end are what the test actually cares about.

A plain mismatch (no ...) produces an index-by-index diff instead of two dumped lists:

path mismatch:
   [0] expected='router' actual='router'
-> [1] expected='escalate' actual='lookup_order'
   [2] expected='refund' actual='<missing>'

Scope limit: only one ... gap is supported. A second one raises ValueError, not a silently-wrong match — two gaps make "which gap swallowed the mismatch?" genuinely ambiguous to report well, and nothing in v0.1's goals needs it.

docs.title: assert_visited / assert_not_visited
docs.text:
assert_visited(traj, "human_approval")
assert_not_visited(traj, "escalate")

Simple membership checks against .path.

docs.title: assert_visits
docs.text:
assert_visits(traj, "retriever", max=2)

Caps how many times a node ran. max only (no min) — that's the direction the use case actually needs (catching an unbounded retry/poll loop); min is a one-line addition the day a test needs it.

docs.title: assert_state / assert_state_at
docs.text:
assert_state(traj, "intent", "refund")                       # final state
assert_state_at(traj, "router", "intent", "refund")           # state right after a node ran
assert_state_at(traj, "retriever", "n", 1, occurrence=0)       # ... after its *first* visit, not its last

assert_state_at's occurrence follows ordinary Python list-indexing: -1 (the default) means "the most recent visit," 0 means "the first." This matters once a node runs more than once — "the state after the router ran" is ambiguous otherwise, and defaulting to the most recent visit matches how people usually phrase it ("after it finally settled").

docs.title: assert_tool_called / assert_tool_not_called
docs.text:
assert_tool_called(traj, "refund_api", args_match={"order_id": "1234"})
assert_tool_called(traj, "refund_api", args_match={"order_id": lambda v: v.startswith("12")})
assert_tool_called(traj, "refund_api", args_match={"request_id": any_str()})
assert_tool_not_called(traj, "delete_account")

args_match only has to name the keys you care about — any key not mentioned is ignored, and a call matches if every mentioned key matches. If a tool was called several times, matching just one call is enough: this checks "this happened at least once," not "this happened exactly this way every time."

Three kinds of value work in args_match:

Value Matches when A plain value ("1234") Exactly equal A callable (lambda v: v > 0) Truthy when called with the real value A Matcher (any_str()) Its own .matches() says yes

any_str() is the one matcher built so far — it matches any string, regardless of content. More (any_int(), any_value(), …) get added the day a real test needs one, not speculatively.

docs.title: assert_retries
docs.text:
assert_retries(traj, "lookup_order", max=1)

Counts how many times a node was re-entered after one of its own tool calls errored — not just how many times it ran. This is narrower than assert_visits on purpose: a node that's a normal loop body (pagination, polling) running many times isn't a retry, it's the design. What this counts is specifically "ran, a tool call inside it failed, and it ran again" — the thing you'd actually want a budget on.

docs.title: assert_interrupted_at
docs.text:
assert_interrupted_at(traj, "human_approval")

Asserts the run paused on a human-in-the-loop interrupt at a specific node (checks both traj.interrupted and that the last step's kind == "interrupt").

docs.title: assert_budget
docs.text:
assert_budget(traj, cost_usd=0.05, latency_s=8, tokens=6000)

Three independent, optional budgets, each checked against the total across the whole run (Trajectory.cost_usd, .latency_s, .tokens_total — see Core concepts), not any single step. Pass only the ones a given test cares about.

docs.title: A note on cost_usd
docs.text: assert_budget's cost_usd check (and Trajectory.cost_usd itself) sums a cost_usd field that's set per LLMCall, not computed by walking a pricing table inside core. See Core concepts: where cost comes from for why that split exists.

docs.title: assert_tool_calls_match
docs.text:
assert_tool_calls_match(traj, ["lookup_order", "refund_api"], mode="strict")
assert_tool_calls_match(traj, other_trajectory, mode="unordered")  # reference can be a Trajectory too

Adopted deliberately from langchain-ai/agentevals' own trajectory-match evaluator, not invented — it's the official LangGraph ecosystem's validated answer to "compare this run against a known-good reference," which nothing else on this page does (the assertions above check specific, known expectations on one trajectory). reference is a plain list of tool names, or another Trajectory (its tool-call names are pulled from it). Matching is by tool name only, not args — assert_tool_called(..., args_match=...) already covers the arg side for one specific call.

Mode Passes when strict Same tool calls as reference, same order unordered Same tool calls (same multiset), any order subset traj only calls tools that appear in reference superset traj calls everything in reference, extra calls allowed

An unrecognized mode raises ValueError immediately, the same "fail loudly on invalid input, don't guess" rule assert_path's multi-gap check follows.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
graphtrace.yaml (project root) is loaded and validated by config.py (pydantic, strict — an unknown field or an invalid value raises pydantic.ValidationError naming the actual field, not a silent ignore). A missing file is normal, not an error: every field falls back to its default.

target: my_app.graph:build_graph    # default factory; "target" not "graph" on purpose —
framework: langgraph                # see Multi-framework support (v0.4) — the only valid value until then, enforced not just documented
replay:
  mode: replay
  cassettes: tests/cassettes/
  normalize:
    - pattern: '\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T[\d:.]+Z'
      replace: '<ts>'
  redact: [api_key, email, phone]
judge:
  model: groq/openai/gpt-oss-120b     # a real, working litellm model string -- this project's own graphtrace.yaml uses exactly this
  rubrics_dir: rubrics/
  calibration_set: evals/calibration.jsonl
  min_agreement: 0.8
budgets:
  default: {cost_usd: 0.10, latency_s: 15}
pricing_overrides: {}
report:
  html: reports/graphtrace.html

docs.title: What's actually enforced today
docs.text:
• framework: pydantic.Literal["langgraph"] — any other value (including crewai/autogen, not built until v0.4) is rejected at load time, not just documented as unsupported.
  • replay.mode: must be one of record/replay/record_missing/live.
  • replay.cassettes: the run_graph pytest fixture uses this as the directory a test's auto-generated cassette path lives under (<cassettes>/<test node id>.yaml).
  • budgets.default: the run_graph fixture applies this automatically after every call, via core/budgets.py's Budgets.check() — a test that never calls assert_budget(...) itself still fails if the configured default is exceeded.
  • judge: requires model if the section is present at all; consulted directly by graphtrace calibrate (judge.model/judge.rubrics_dir/judge.calibration_set/judge.min_agreement) — see Judge & calibration.
  • report: report.html is the default output path for graphtrace report when --out isn't given — see Report & CI.

docs.title: Still planned
docs.text:
Planned — not built yet

  • replay.normalize's custom rules aren't wired through to core/normalize.py yet (the built-in timestamp/UUID rules are, and are used for every cassette match).
  • replay.redact isn't enforced — see Recording & replay for the current state of this gap.
  • pricing_overrides isn't read by frameworks/pricing.py yet.

docs.title: Cut-point replay (v0.2)
docs.text:
Planned for v0.2 — not built, and gated on v0.1 shipping first

Nothing on this page is implemented. See Roadmap & status.

docs.title: What it's for
docs.text:
A production incident happens. You record it as a cassette. You fix the code. Now you want to know: does the fix actually work — not "does replaying the exact same broken run still look broken," which is all plain replay mode can tell you.

cut mode answers that: replay the recorded incident up to the point it went wrong, then run the fixed code live from there. Everything before the cut point is free and instant (served from the cassette); everything after is real, because that's the part actually being tested.

run_graph(graph, inputs, cassette="incident_2026_11_03.yaml", mode="cut", cut_at="lookup_order")

Produces an ordinary Trajectory — every existing assert_* function works against it unmodified.

docs.title: Where this comes from
docs.text: Adopted deliberately from Chronicle (Microsoft, arXiv 2609.20625), which reports: bit-stable replay across 20 repetitions, zero model calls on the replayed portion, and — in a mutation-testing study — catching every mutant that let a recorded unsafe action through, where naively stubbing every boundary caught none. That last result is the actual evidence this is worth adopting: a cruder "replay everything, assert the final state" approach misses exactly the kind of regression cut-point replay is designed to catch.

docs.title: What happens if the recording and the live run disagree before the cut point
docs.text: The run fails loudly — "recorded run diverged before the cut point" — rather than silently serving a stale cassette entry. If a loop now runs a different number of times, or a retry was added or removed, that's a sign the recording no longer describes what's actually happening up to the cut, and trusting it past that point would validate the fix against the wrong starting state.

docs.title: Relationship to trace-to-test
docs.text: Trace-to-test already turns a production trace into a cassette and a generated test. cut mode is what makes that generated test useful for verifying a fix, not just for locking in whatever the agent currently does (which might still be the bug).

docs.title: Judge & calibration
docs.text:
A judge call via litellm (so any provider works), with the model id pinned in graphtrace.yaml's judge.model — never left to drift silently. Rubric files are small YAML documents: a list of pass/fail criteria the judge is asked to grade against, nothing invented beyond them.

# rubrics/refund_reply.yaml
id: refund_reply
version: 1
criteria:
  - id: confirms_amount
    description: Reply states the refund amount.
  - id: no_promises
    description: Reply does not promise a specific delivery timeline.
scale: pass_fail
pass_threshold: all

judge/client.py's JudgeClient.ask_json() forces JSON output (response_format={"type": "json_object"}), retries exactly once on a malformed response, then raises JudgeError — never a silent None standing in for "the judge didn't answer properly." litellm is imported lazily, inside that one method — constructing a JudgeClient, or hitting a cassette-replayed verdict in replay mode, never requires litellm to be installed at all.

docs.title: Judge verdicts are cached like any other call
docs.text:
judge/client.py's grade() reuses replay/engine.py's resolve_call() directly — the exact same cassette/replay machinery an LLM or tool call goes through. A judge verdict is keyed by (rubric.id, "judge", request), the same way an LLM call is keyed by (node, "llm", messages). The practical effect: once a judge call is recorded, a replay-mode test run never calls the judge again — grading stays free and deterministic in CI the same way the rest of the test is.

Only scale: pass_fail rubrics are actually scored today. A scale: "1-5" rubric loads and validates (so a project can write one ahead of need), but grade() raises NotImplementedError rather than guessing a pass/fail threshold from a 1–5 scale that was never designed.

docs.title: graphtrace calibrate
docs.text:
graphtrace calibrate --rubric refund_reply

Scores the judge against graphtrace.yaml's judge.calibration_set — a JSONL file, one case per line, each holding rubric, input, output, and a human dict of ground-truth labels per criterion:

{"rubric": "refund_reply", "input": "can I get a refund?", "output": "yes, $49.00 refunded", "human": {"confirms_amount": true, "no_promises": true}}

judge/calibrate.py reports agreement % and Cohen's kappa per criterion — not one overall number, since different criteria genuinely have different reliability. Calibration always calls the real judge, never a cassette: caching a calibration run would defeat the entire point of it (confirming the judge's current real behaviour against human judgment).

The CLI exits non-zero when any criterion with at least one labelled case falls below judge.min_agreement — the gate a CI pipeline would actually check. A criterion with zero labelled cases is reported and skipped, not silently treated as a pass or a failure.

A case the judge fails to answer (a malformed response even after the one retry) is skipped for that criterion's tally, not counted as disagreement — a JudgeError is itself a signal the judge is broken for that input, and low agreement should already surface that; double-penalizing the same underlying problem would just make the number harder to read.

docs.title: A real correction, found by checking the math by hand
docs.text:
This project's own internal build plan originally claimed "full disagreement scores kappa 0.0." That's wrong for balanced labels, and it was caught before anything shipped: a perfect inversion (every human True judged False and vice versa, on a balanced 2-2 split) scores kappa = -1.0, not 0.0 — a real, measurable anti-correlation, worse than chance, not merely "no better than chance." Verified by hand against the actual formula (κ = (p₀ − pₑ)/(1 − pₑ)) and against the real installed sklearn.metrics.cohen_kappa_score, not assumed from the inherited phrasing.

Kappa 0.0 — genuine chance-level agreement — needs a case with real, independent variance on both sides (e.g. human [True, True, False, False] vs. judge [True, False, True, False]), not a systematic flip. The distinction matters for reading your own calibration numbers: a kappa near -1 is a sharper, more specific warning sign ("the judge is anti-correlated with human judgment, maybe the rubric criterion is phrased backwards") than a kappa near 0 ("the judge adds no information").

docs.title: Multi-framework support: CrewAI & AutoGen (v0.4)
docs.text:
Planned for v0.4 — not built, and gated on v0.1 shipping first

Nothing on this page is implemented. v0.1 is LangGraph-only. See Roadmap & status.

docs.title: Why v0.1 is LangGraph-only, and what "later" actually means
docs.text: v0.1's goals are scoped to LangGraph. Non-LangGraph framework support was originally written into the plan as a loose aspiration ("these can come later") with no version and no design — as of 2026-10-21, it's a real, designed phase: v0.4, with the one architecture decision it needs already made in v0.1 itself (see below), not deferred.

docs.title: What stays unchanged (the part of "framework-agnostic" that was already true)
docs.text: core/ — the Trajectory/Step data model, all 12 assert_* functions, budgets, errors, matchers — needs zero changes for CrewAI or AutoGen support. Every field is already generic enough (plain dict[str, Any] state, a plain tuple[str, ...] namespace) to represent a different framework's execution. This is also the real test of the design: if adding a framework ever turns out to require a core/ change, that's a bug in this claim, not a reason to quietly patch around it.

docs.title: What v0.1 changes proactively, ahead of needing it
docs.text: The LangGraph-specific recording layer is built as frameworks/base.py (a shared FrameworkRunner Protocol) + frameworks/langgraph/ (the only real implementation until v0.4) — not as a flat, LangGraph-only runtime/ package that would need renaming later. Config and CLI already use generic names (target:/framework: instead of graph:; --target instead of --graph) even though langgraph is the only valid framework value today.

docs.title: What v0.4 actually has to build
docs.text:
• frameworks/crewai/ and frameworks/autogen/ — each a full runner.py/recorder.py/interceptors.py, implementing the same Protocol.
  • Interceptors are per-framework, not shared. CrewAI and AutoGen don't reliably go through the LangChain classes graphtrace's LangGraph interceptor patches — each framework gets its own real patch target, confirmed against the installed library version at build time, not assumed in advance.
  • An open design question, not yet answered: AutoGen group chats can rotate speakers dynamically, by design. Whether that fits assert_path's current exact-match/single-...-gap model, needs a new assertion, or is a documented scope limit for open-ended group chats specifically, is decided against a real example when this gets built — not guessed now.

The full design — the concept-mapping table (how each framework's execution maps onto Step/Trajectory), the reasoning for per-framework interceptors, and the weekwise build order — lives in the project's own internal plan doc, not published here.

docs.title: Observability export (v0.2)

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Trace-to-test pulls traces in from observability tools to build tests. This closes the loop the other way: pushing graphtrace's own results out, so a nightly live run shows up as a quality signal next to an app's real production traces, not just as a CI artifact nobody reopens once the build goes green.

  • Mapped from the existing per-test JSON result — no new data model: test name/node path becomes a span name/attributes, pass/fail becomes span status, cost_usd/latency_s/tokens_total become span metrics, a judge verdict becomes a span attribute, a budget breach becomes a span event.
  • Exporters: OpenTelemetry (OTLP), Langfuse (one trace per test, scored per rubric), or a generic webhook.
  • Export is opt-in and off by default, best-effort (a failed export logs a warning, never fails the test), and runs through the same redaction hook cassettes use before anything leaves the local machine.

docs.title: run_graph / arun_graph — real, tested
docs.text:
from graphtrace import run_graph

traj = run_graph(graph, inputs, cassette="tests/cassettes/my_test.yaml", mode="record", resume=[True])

run_graph(graph, inputs, *, cassette, config=None, thread_id="gc-test", resume=None, mode=None) -> Trajectory (and an async arun_graph) drives a compiled LangGraph via graph.stream(..., stream_mode=["debug"], subgraphs=True), feeding every event to a recorder that builds up a Trajectory. A MemorySaver checkpointer is attached automatically if the graph doesn't already have one. resume is a list of values fed to successive human-in-the-loop interrupts, one per pause, in order — if the graph pauses and there's no next value queued, run_graph stops there and returns with interrupted=True.

mode resolves via an explicit argument, then the GRAPHTRACE_MODE environment variable, then "live" — unchanged Week 1 behaviour unless something actually opts in. Through the run_graph pytest fixture, it also resolves from pytest --gt-mode=<mode>.

Subgraphs (a node whose value is itself a compiled graph) are handled transparently, not collapsed into one opaque step. Step.kind gets a subgraph_enter step the moment the recorder detects a wrapping node (a child event arrives at a namespace that extends it), its own inner nodes become ordinary "node" steps in between, and a subgraph_exit step closes it out once the wrapping task's own checkpoint finally settles (necessarily last, since a subgraph's own completion can't be known before its children's). A real tool/LLM call made inside a subgraph's own node is attributed to that inner node directly, not lost or misattributed to the wrapper — confirmed by hand that langgraph_checkpoint_ns chains as "sub:<id>|inner_a:<id>", and the existing rsplit(':', 1) attribution logic already extracts the innermost id correctly regardless of nesting depth. A real bug was found and fixed getting here: the recorder's state bookkeeping used to be global, single-namespace state, so a subgraph running concurrently with another outer-level node (parallel fan-out) could corrupt that sibling's recorded state with the subgraph's own unrelated partial state — fixed by scoping all of it per namespace. See tests/test_runner.py's two subgraph tests, each confirmed to genuinely fail against the pre-fix recorder.

docs.title: The four modes — real, tested
docs.text:
Mode LLM/tool calls? Cassette replay No Must exist; a missing entry raises CassetteMismatchError record Yes Overwritten record_missing Only for unmatched requests Appended live (default) Yes Ignored entirely 
# Record once (real calls happen, a cassette gets written):
run_graph(graph, inputs, cassette="tests/cassettes/happy_path.yaml", mode="record")

# Replay it later -- zero real calls, verified by patching the real underlying
# LangChain methods to raise if they're ever actually reached (tests/test_mode_aware_interceptors.py):
run_graph(graph, inputs, cassette="tests/cassettes/happy_path.yaml", mode="replay")

A replayed failure (a tool call that errored when it was recorded) re-raises as a plain RuntimeError carrying the original error message — the original exception's exact type isn't recoverable once serialized to YAML, an honest, documented limitation rather than a bug. A live exception (not from a cassette) always keeps its real type, so a node's own except SomeSpecificError: still works identically in every mode.

docs.title: Cassette format — real
docs.text:
A real cassette, recorded from examples/refund_agent (field order exactly as graphtrace itself writes it, not reordered for the doc):

version: 1
graphtrace: 0.1.0
recorded_at: '2026-10-21T06:57:12.584162+00:00'
entries:
- key: router/llm/391132dd9ec5/0
  kind: llm
  node: router
  request: "[('human', 'What does the customer want for order 1234?')]"
  latency_s: 0.0021508999925572425
  response:
    content: ok
    tool_calls: []
    usage:
      input_tokens: 0
      output_tokens: 0
  model: GenericFakeChatModel
- key: lookup_order/tool/82eee3ce806e/0
  kind: tool
  node: lookup_order
  request:
    order_id: '1234'
  latency_s: 0.0006061000167392194
  response:
    status: delivered
    amount: 49.0
  name: get_order

YAML via ruamel.yaml's round-trip mode, loaded and saved through replay/cassette.py — proven byte-identical on a load-then-immediately-save round trip (not just that the library loaded without erroring), which is what actually makes record_missing growing a cassette produce a clean PR diff: untouched entries stay untouched bytes.

The matching key is node/kind/hash(normalized request)/occurrence (replay/matcher.py) — occurrence is what lets the same node+request pair appear twice in one run (a retry loop) and still match its own two separate recorded entries, in order, confirmed with a real recorded-then-replayed retry sequence.

A real bug found and fixed along the way: ruamel.yaml's round-trip mode wraps a loaded float (49.0) in a ScalarFloat subclass, to preserve its exact on-disk formatting. That's essential for the byte-identical round-trip above — but the same value, handed back into a replayed tool call, flows straight into LangGraph's own state and gets msgpack-serialized by its checkpointer, which doesn't know what a ScalarFloat is and raises TypeError: Type is not msgpack serializable. Confirmed by hand, not assumed. Fixed with replay/cassette.to_plain_python(), called only on a value about to flow back into real code — never on a value still destined for the cassette file itself, which is what keeps the round-trip guarantee above true at the same time.

docs.title: Still planned
docs.text:
Planned — not built yet

  • Redaction. The architecture plan's own redact: [api_key, email, phone] config field isn't enforced by anything yet — a recorded cassette today contains whatever the real request/response actually held, unmasked. Treat any cassette containing real secrets as sensitive until this exists.
  • Normalization rules beyond the built-in timestamp/UUID pair (core/normalize.py has the mechanism; graphtrace.yaml's replay.normalize list of custom rules isn't wired through to it yet).
  • cut mode (v0.2 — see Cut-point replay).

docs.title: Why this was the hard part
docs.text: Turning a real LangGraph run into a correct Trajectory needed two real corrections to the original design along the way — not assumptions that happened to be wrong in theory, but things confirmed wrong by running real code: the originally-planned contextvars call-attribution mechanism doesn't survive LangGraph's actual ThreadPoolExecutor-based parallel execution, and the originally-planned _generate/_agenerate patch target is never actually called by any real chat model. Both are detailed in the project's internal plan doc, along with the ScalarFloat finding above.

docs.title: Statistical live-mode verification (v0.2)
docs.text:
Planned for v0.2 — not built, and not scheduled for v0.1

A single live-mode run is a single run, pass or fail — not strong evidence on its own, since real models are genuinely non-deterministic. assert_live_stable(target, inputs, trials=50, pass_threshold=0.85, alpha=0.05, check=...) (adopted from AgentAssay, arXiv 2603.02601) runs the same call repeatedly and reports Pass / Fail / Inconclusive from a Wilson-score confidence interval on the pass rate — refusing to force a binary call when there isn't yet enough evidence, rather than trusting a raw percentage that can look fine while actually being too close to call. Scoped to opt-in, scheduled drift checks only (each trial is a real, billed call) — never the default PR path.

docs.title: Report & CI
docs.text:
pytest --gt-mode=replay --gt-report=reports/graphtrace.html

A pytest hook (plugin.py's pytest_runtest_makereport/pytest_sessionfinish) collects one TestResult per test and, at session end, renders a static HTML page from them — one entry per test, an expandable trajectory tree, judge verdicts with their reasons, cost/latency/token totals. No server, no hosted dashboard, by design. A results.json is written alongside the HTML (same path, .json extension) — graphtrace report results.json re-renders the HTML from it standalone, for re-rendering later or merging results across CI shards without re-running anything.

Every test that calls the run_graph fixture gets its real Trajectory attached to its report entry automatically — no extra code in the test itself. A test that fails before its body even runs (a broken fixture) is still reported, as "error" rather than "failed", with no trajectory to show (there wasn't one to capture) but with the real failure message.

docs.title: What the report shows
docs.text:
The report is laid out in two layers, for two different readers:

  • Executive summary (always visible, no detail hidden behind a click): a release verdict — READY or NOT READY, N blocking issues — a ranked list of blocking issues (most severe first), and a coverage breakdown by category. This is the layer a QA lead, manager, consultant, or auditor actually needs to make a go/no-go call, without reading a single trajectory. See Executive summary metadata below for how to feed it real descriptions, severities, and categories instead of raw test names.
  • Technical detail (collapsed by default, under a disclosure triangle): the same per-test trajectory tree this report has always had — every step's node, kind, latency, each LLM call (model, token counts, cost, output), each tool call (name, args, result or error), and judge verdicts with their reasons. This is the engineer's layer, for debugging why something failed once the summary says something needs attention.
  • Summary row: total/passed/failed/errored counts, total cost (USD) and total latency across every test.
  • Rendered via Jinja2 with autoescape=True, passed explicitly and unconditionally — not inferred from the template's filename. Trajectory state, tool args/results, an LLM's own output, and now a test's own description/category can all hold arbitrary data (a user's refund note, a crafted prompt injection attempt...), the same XSS concern kbguard's own report has. Confirmed with real tests that a <script> tag anywhere in any of these renders as escaped text, never live markup.

docs.title: Executive summary metadata: @pytest.mark.graphtrace(...)
docs.text:
Without this, the blocking-issues list falls back to showing a bare test_id — technically accurate, meaningless to anyone who doesn't already know what that test checks. Tag a test to make its entry readable by someone who doesn't read code:

@pytest.mark.graphtrace(
    description="Customer should not be refunded without human approval",
    severity="critical",  # "critical" | "high" | "normal" (default) | "low"
    category="safety",    # any free-form string -- grouped into the coverage breakdown
)
def test_refund_requires_approval(run_graph):
    ...

All three are optional, and the marker is registered (plugin.py's pytest_configure) so using it never triggers pytest's own "unknown marker" warning. An untagged test still reports correctly — severity defaults to "normal", description/category fall back to showing the bare test id — so adopting this is additive, not required before the report shows any value at all.

Severity never decides whether a failure blocks release — only how it's ranked and visually emphasized among real failures. Graphtrace has no basis to decide a "low" severity failure is safe to ship anyway; that's a human call the report surfaces clearly (a red-bordered entry, last in the list) rather than one it ever makes for you. The verdict is simply: any failed or errored test means NOT READY, full stop.

Coverage is the set of distinct category values seen across the whole run, with counts — a quick answer to "what did this actually test," not just "how many things passed." If nothing in the run was tagged with a category, the report says so honestly (coverage breakdown unavailable) instead of fabricating one from test names.

Not yet built, and worth knowing before expecting it: a trend view across multiple runs ("better or worse than last time") would need a separate persistence design — where run history lives, how many runs to keep, whether it's per-branch — and isn't attempted here. Today's report is a single run's snapshot, full stop; comparing it to a previous one is still a manual, outside-the-report job.

docs.title: CI
docs.text:
JUnit XML comes for free from pytest — no extra work needed for a CI dashboard to pick results up alongside (or instead of) the HTML report. .github/workflows/graphtrace.yml runs pytest (every test in this repo's own suite runs against fake chat models, so no provider key is needed) and mkdocs build --strict on every push/PR — graphtrace testing itself with its own tools, the same gate kbguard uses, scoped to what's actually configured here today (no ruff/mypy step — neither is wired up in this project yet, and a gate with nothing behind it would just be a step that always passes without checking anything).

A separate nightly --gt-mode=live workflow (catching real drift against real models) is documented here as the intended pattern but not itself built — it needs a real provider account and key to mean anything, and this project doesn't want to claim a workflow is "real" when it would do nothing without secrets nobody's configured yet.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
Red-teaming an agent using the same trajectory/cassette/assertions core v0.1 builds — an attack is just a cassette entry with adversarial content planted in it, no new runtime required.

  • Attack classes: direct prompt injection (user message), indirect/tool-result injection (a poisoned tool response), tool poisoning (a malicious tool description), data exfiltration, and a "canary" disallowed action that must never fire.
  • Payload library: seeded from public taxonomies (OWASP's LLM injection patterns, a curated subset of garak/PyRIT probes) rather than hand-invented strings, versioned the same way rubrics are.
  • Assertions: assert_resisted_injection, assert_no_canary_fired, assert_no_data_leak(patterns=[...]) — softer judgments (half-compliance, "apologizes then does it anyway") go through the same judge contract with a dedicated rubric class.
  • Runs as its own graphtrace redteam command, or as a marked pytest suite (@pytest.mark.graphtrace_security) for teams that want it on every PR rather than gated to pre-release.

docs.title: Trace-to-test
docs.text:
graphtrace from-trace trace.json --target my_app.graph:build_graph

Turns a production trace export (Langfuse, OTel/OpenInference, or LangSmith) into:

  • a cassette built from the trace's LLM and tool spans, and
  • a generated pytest file that replays that run and asserts the nodes it actually visited, with a # TODO: assert the correct behaviour marker where you fill in what should have happened.

A trace importer only has to implement one small protocol (can_read, to_normalized) — adding a new source is one file (importers/<name>.py), not a change to codegen/test_writer.py's own conversion logic. All three bundled importers converge on one shared NormalizedTrace/NormalizedSpan shape (importers/base.py).

None of the three bundled importers are verified against a live export from a real account — each one's own module docstring says exactly what's confirmed against that platform's documented export format versus representative-but-unverified, rather than overclaiming. Verify field names against a real export from your own project before trusting an importer beyond the bundled test fixtures, especially Langfuse's, whose data model has moved fast.

docs.title: Why the generated assertion is "visited", not the exact path
docs.text:
A trace importer only ever sees LLM and tool calls — a node that makes neither (a pure routing branch, a human-in-the-loop interrupt point) is invisible to every source platform's own export, not just to graphtrace's reading of it. Asserting the exact sequence of every node visited (assert_path) from an imported trace would therefore be a false promise: it would claim knowledge the trace never actually contained.

The generated test asserts assert_visited(trajectory, node) for each node that made a captured call instead — true, but deliberately looser than what assert_path can check. Once you know the real path, tighten the generated test by hand with assert_path(...) or assert_tool_calls_match(...) — both are regular graphtrace assertions, nothing generated-test-specific about them.

docs.title: A real limit, not an oversight
docs.text: If the trace includes a human-in-the-loop interrupt, the generated test gets a resume=[...] # TODO: fill in what the human actually sent stub instead of a guessed value. A resume payload genuinely isn't recoverable from the trace alone — the generated test is deliberately left needing that fill-in, rather than silently guessing wrong. In practice this field is always unset today: none of Langfuse/OTel/LangSmith's own export formats carry a universal "this run paused for human input" concept to detect it from (NormalizedTrace.interrupted defaults to False, documented as an open gap in importers/base.py). A trace whose original run really did pause and resume still generates a usable test either way — replaying it with no resume value simply reproduces the same pause, and the generated assertions (only ever about nodes visited before that point) still hold.

docs.title: A factory that needs real arguments
docs.text:
A LangGraph builder function commonly takes a chat model (or other required config) as an argument — this project's own demo agent, build_refund_graph(chat_model, ...), is written exactly that way. from-trace actually imports your real --target and inspects its signature before generating anything: a factory with any required parameter gets

graph = build_graph(...)  # TODO: this factory takes required arguments graphtrace can't know from the trace alone (e.g. a chat model) -- construct it the way your app really does

instead of a wrong, silently-broken build_graph(). A target that genuinely can't be imported at all (wrong --target, module not yet on the path) gets the same cautious placeholder, for the same reason: there's no way to know what it needs, and the generated file's own top-level import line surfaces the real problem either way.

docs.title: The cassette this produces doesn't hash-match like other cassettes
docs.text:
Every other cassette in this project matches a call by hashing its exact request (node/kind/hash(request)/occurrence) — a real retry against the real graph reproduces the same request, so the hash matches. An imported trace's own request field is whatever shape the source platform exported it in (Langfuse's JSON, an OTel attribute string, ...), which is never the same shape as the real str(list[BaseMessage]) the live LangGraph interceptor hashes at replay time. There's no general transformation between the two.

from-trace's cassettes use a position-only fallback instead — a literal any hash segment (node/kind/any/occurrence), matched by replay/engine.py only when the exact-hash lookup already missed, so it can never shadow a real recorded entry from a normal record-mode cassette. It trades exact-request verification for trusting the target graph to walk the same node sequence for the same initial_input — which is exactly what "replay the observed run" means for an imported trace, no more.

docs.title: Core concepts: Trajectory & Step
docs.text: Implemented and tested (src/graphtrace/core/trajectory.py, tests/test_trajectory.py). Nothing on this page touches LangGraph — that's the point, see Why core stays framework-agnostic below.

docs.title: The shape
docs.text:
@dataclass
class LLMCall:
    node: str
    model: str
    input_hash: str
    prompt_tokens: int
    completion_tokens: int
    latency_s: float
    output: Any
    cost_usd: float = 0.0

@dataclass
class ToolCall:
    node: str
    name: str
    args: dict[str, Any]
    result: Any
    error: str | None
    latency_s: float

@dataclass
class Step:
    index: int
    node: str
    kind: Literal["node", "interrupt", "subgraph_enter", "subgraph_exit"]
    state_before: dict[str, Any]
    state_after: dict[str, Any]
    state_diff: dict[str, Any]
    llm_calls: list[LLMCall] = field(default_factory=list)
    tool_calls: list[ToolCall] = field(default_factory=list)
    namespace: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    latency_s: float = 0.0

@dataclass
class Trajectory:
    steps: list[Step]
    final_state: dict[str, Any]
    interrupted: bool
    mode: Literal["record", "replay", "live"]

A Trajectory is one recorded run: every node visited (steps), in order, each carrying its own state transition and whatever it called.

docs.title: Derived properties
docs.text: Property / method Returns .path list[str] of node names, in order — what assert_path checks .visits(node) How many times node appears in .path .tool_calls / .llm_calls Every call of that kind across every step, flattened, in order .final_message The last message's text content, if the state has a messages key (supports both LangChain message objects and plain dicts) .cost_usd Sum of every LLMCall.cost_usd in the run .latency_s Sum of every Step.latency_s .tokens_total Sum of every LLMCall.prompt_tokens + completion_tokens

docs.title: Why core stays framework-agnostic
docs.text:
Nothing in graphtrace.core may import LangGraph, an LLM SDK, or anything from graphtrace.runtime (the layer, not yet built, that will actually run a LangGraph and produce one of these). A Trajectory is plain dataclasses and plain Python values — lists, dicts, strings, floats — on purpose:

  • Everything downstream only ever needs a Trajectory. Assertions, budgets, and the eventual HTML report don't know or care whether it came from a real LangGraph run or was built by hand in a test (see the Quickstart, which does exactly that).
  • A future non-LangGraph adapter costs nothing extra here. If graphtrace ever grows a CrewAI or AutoGen adapter, it only has to produce a Trajectory too — nothing in this file, or in assertions.py, would need to change.

docs.title: Where cost comes from
docs.text:
LLMCall.cost_usd is a plain field, not something Trajectory computes on the fly. This is a deliberate fix relative to the project's original architecture plan, which had Trajectory.cost_usd reach into a runtime/pricing.py token→USD table directly — that would mean core importing from runtime, which breaks the rule above. Instead, the (not-yet-built) recorder will resolve a cost in dollars at record time and set LLMCall.cost_usd once; Trajectory.cost_usd just sums it:

@property
def cost_usd(self) -> float:
    return sum(call.cost_usd for call in self.llm_calls)

A hand-built LLMCall in a test can simply leave cost_usd at its default of 0.0 if cost isn't what that test is checking.

docs.title: Case study: catching what a "looks right" LangGraph agent hides
Why I built this
docs.text:
Most agent frameworks make it easy to check whether the final answer looks right, and hard to check whether the agent got there safely. A LangGraph agent with branches, retries and tool calls can pass every day while a retry quietly starts firing on every call, a tool stops being invoked, or an approval step gets routed around — none of which shows up if a test only checks the text that comes out at the end.

I wanted to test the path itself, not just the destination: which nodes ran, in what order, what each one changed, what it called — asserted directly, the way a web framework lets you check a response's status code and not just the rendered page. And I wanted it proven on real agents, not a demo built to flatter the tool, so once the core worked I pointed it at two real open-source LangGraph projects and let them find what my own test fixtures couldn't.

docs.title: What I set out to do
docs.text:
• Record a full run — every node, state change, tool call and LLM call — without touching the agent's own code.
  • Give it a small set of readable assertions, not a dump of raw trace data to dig through by hand.
  • Make a recorded run replay with zero real LLM calls, so CI never pays for, or waits on, a real model to pass.
  • Add an LLM-as-judge for what a plain assertion can't cover, calibrated against real human labels first — never trusted blindly.
  • Validate it against real external agents before calling it done.

docs.title: How it's put together
docs.text:
• Framework-agnostic core. The trajectory model and assertion API know nothing about LangGraph specifically — they're built against a plain data structure, so this isn't locked to one framework.
  • No changes to the agent under test. Recording works by patching the framework's own calls for the duration of a run, undone automatically when it ends.
  • Record once, replay for free. A run is written to a plain YAML file and replayed from it afterward — no real network calls, no bill, on every CI run after the first recording.
  • Real numbers, not estimates. Cost and latency come from what was actually recorded.
  • Judge calibration before trust. An LLM-as-judge verdict is scored against a human-labelled set with Cohen's kappa before it's relied on for anything.

docs.title: Problems I ran into
docs.text:
• A concurrency assumption that didn't hold. The first design tracked "which node is running" with a thread-local variable. LangGraph runs parallel nodes on worker threads that don't inherit it. Fixed by reading the node/task id LangGraph already attaches to every call — no workaround needed once I found it.
  • Patching the wrong method. Intercepting chat-model calls meant patching a base-class method. Every real chat model overrides that method with its own version, so the patch caught nothing. Fixed by patching the actual methods every real model defines.
  • A YAML feature that broke LangGraph's own state. Round-trip YAML mode wraps numbers in a type that preserves formatting — which LangGraph's checkpointer didn't recognize and rejected the moment a recorded value replayed back into a real run. Fixed by converting back to plain types right before a value re-enters real code.
  • A statistic I had wrong. Cohen's kappa doesn't score 0.0 for "complete disagreement" — a systematic reversal scores -1.0, a real negative correlation and a far stronger signal than "no agreement at all." Corrected the calibration report to reflect that.
  • A feature that was designed but never built. The data model had room for sub-agent enter/exit steps from week one; nothing produced them, because nothing tested a node that's itself another graph. Building it surfaced a worse bug: state tracking was shared globally instead of scoped per sub-agent, so two sub-agents running at once could corrupt each other's recorded data. Fixed by scoping it per sub-agent.

docs.title: What it found once I pointed it at real agents
docs.text:
Once the core held up against my own demo agent, I ran it against two real, official open-source LangGraph projects — langgraph-swarm-py and deepagents — across 25 scenarios built from their own test suites, not invented ones:

Project What it found langgraph-swarm-py Tool calls attributed to the wrong node — a newer LangChain agent abstraction had stopped passing an explicit config the recorder relied on. langgraph-swarm-py Sub-agent enter/exit markers recorded in the wrong order. langgraph-swarm-py A real agent-to-agent handoff crashed recording outright — the handoff object wasn't safe to write to YAML. deepagents A tool's runtime object leaked internal state (object ids, open file handles) into recordings, so the same logical call hashed differently every run.

One real limitation surfaced too, not a bug: a tool that internally calls another LangGraph agent loses that nested agent's step-by-step detail on replay — the final answer is still correct, just not the path that produced it. Documented rather than hidden.

docs.title: What it looks like now
docs.text:
• 222 tests pass — the core recording/replay/assertion/judge/report pipeline, plus the 25 real-agent scenarios above.
  • Published on PyPI. pip install graphtrace registers it as a pytest plugin automatically.
  • A CLI turns a real exported production trace into a generated test; a static HTML report gives a plain pass/fail verdict for anyone who isn't the engineer who wrote the test.
  • CI runs the full suite and a strict documentation build on every push.

docs.title: If you're running an agent like this
docs.text:
Wrong node attribution, steps recorded out of order, a crash on a real handoff, a cache key that silently broke between runs — four real bugs, found in real, official open-source projects, and every one of them came from a system that already had passing tests. That's exactly the kind of gap that stays invisible until someone checks the actual path, not just the output. If you're running a LangGraph agent, or anything with the same branches/retries/tool-calls shape, in production or about to put one there, it's worth asking whether your current tests would catch any of that. Most wouldn't — they're built to check the answer, not the route it took to get there.

graphtrace is open source and ready to point at your own graph, with no changes needed to the agent itself: github.com/devbyanoop/graphtrace.

I'm available for freelance work in test automation and AI-agent testing, from framework design to hardening an existing agent for production. You can reach me through my GitHub profile.

docs.title: Fixed (2026-10-26) -- found testing against a real external app, not graphtrace's own demo agent
docs.text:
run_graph() pointed at a real, official LangGraph app for the first time -- langchain-ai/langgraph-swarm-py (the LangGraph team's own multi-agent swarm library) -- rather than examples/refund_agent, which was hand-written specifically to exercise graphtrace's own features and so never could have surfaced these. Kept as a permanent regression test, tests/test_langgraph_swarm_compat.py, gated with pytest.importorskip behind the dev extra's new langgraph-swarm dependency.

  • LangChain 1.x's create_agent() doesn't thread an explicit config into its model call. Every LLM call was attributed to node "?" -- confirmed by hand that BaseChatModel.invoke() receives config=None under this newer agent abstraction, with the real metadata reachable only through LangChain's own ambient, contextvar-based config propagation. Fixed in frameworks/langgraph/interceptors.py by resolving metadata through ensure_config(config) instead of reading config directly; what's forwarded to the real underlying call is untouched.
  • A subgraph's subgraph_enter/subgraph_exit step pair had their index values backwards (exit lower than its own enter) -- the previous day's subgraph fix created a new, later-indexed step for the enter marker while the exit kept the parent's original, earlier one. Fixed in frameworks/langgraph/recorder.py by swapping which step plays which role.
  • A tool call returning Command(graph=Command.PARENT, ...) (LangGraph's real handoff mechanism) never gets its own task_result/checkpoint, silently dropping the step. Fixed by absorbing any task still pending under a resolving task's own namespace the instant that resolution happens. A related bug found at the same time: neither the tool's real args (which can carry an entire injected graph state, including raw BaseMessage objects) nor a real Command result were YAML-safe, crashing cassette writes. Fixed with a generic, recursive serializer (_yaml_safe/_restore_value) that round-trips BaseMessage and Command correctly through replay -- a real node's own isinstance(result, Command) check still sees a real Command object after a replay, not a plain dict.

181 tests pass, full regression.

docs.title: Added (2026-10-27) -- an executive summary layer for the HTML report
docs.text:
Asked directly who actually reads the HTML report besides an engineer debugging a failure -- the honest answer was nobody, since it was raw trajectory dumps, internal jargon, and stack-trace-style error strings throughout. Added a layer above the existing detail, not a replacement for it:

  • @pytest.mark.graphtrace(description=None, severity='normal', category=None) -- optional per-test metadata, registered in plugin.py so using it never triggers pytest's own "unknown marker" warning. report/results.py's TestResult gained matching description/severity/category fields.
  • report/results.py::build_executive_summary() -- a release verdict (ready iff nothing failed/errored), blocking issues sorted by severity (critical first; any failure blocks regardless of severity -- severity only ranks among real failures, graphtrace never decides one is "safe to ship anyway"), and a category coverage breakdown that honestly says coverage breakdown unavailable rather than fabricating one when nothing was tagged.
  • report/templates/report.html.j2 restructured: the verdict, blocking-issues list, and coverage breakdown render first and are always visible; the existing per-test trajectory tree, judge verdicts, and raw calls moved under a collapsed <details> disclosure below.
  • examples/sample_report/ regenerated with real descriptions/severities/categories on all three sample results, so the portfolio artifact demonstrates this rather than falling back to bare test ids.

Deliberately not attempted: a trend view across multiple runs. That needs its own persistence design (where run history lives, how many runs to keep, per-branch or not) that hasn't been designed, let alone built.

25 new tests (test_report.py), 3 new (test_plugin.py, the marker itself via pytester). 199 tests pass, full regression.

docs.title: Fixed (2026-10-27) -- a second real external app, langchain-ai/deepagents (~30.6k stars)
docs.text:
A different way of using a subgraph than langgraph-swarm-py's: the sub-agent here is invoked from inside a plain tool function (task), not added as a graph node. Kept as a permanent regression test, tests/test_deepagents_compat.py (gated with pytest.importorskip, deepagents added as a second dev-extra compatibility dependency).

  • ToolRuntime carries the entire live Pregel execution state as its config field (per-run object ids, open file/thread handles, functools.partials) -- made the recorded cassette entry for the exact same logical call hash differently across two separate processes, and bloated the cassette into something unreadable. A related bug found one step later, generating a report from this exact test: the same raw dump was landing in the in-memory Trajectory itself (ToolCall.args), since only the copy passed to the cassette writer had been sanitized, not the object the report (and anything else) reads directly. Fixed in both places: _yaml_safe() now recognizes ToolRuntime (lazily imported, never a hard dependency), keeping only state and tool_call_id.
  • Documented, not patched around: a tool whose own implementation triggers a nested LangGraph execution loses that nested execution's step-by-step visibility in replay mode, since replaying the tool call means its real body -- including its own compiled_subagent.invoke(...) call -- never executes. The parent's real-world outcome is identical either way; only the fine-grained trace of how the sub-agent got there is unrecoverable from a cassette. A real fix would mean recursively intercepting calls made from inside an already-intercepted call -- a genuinely different, larger feature, not a quick correction. Confirmed with a real assertion (record mode sees the nested step, replay mode doesn't, both reach the same final message), not left as prose that could go stale.

201 tests pass, full regression.

docs.title: Added (2026-10-27) -- real test depth, not just test count
docs.text:
Asked directly whether 3 thin, mostly happy-path tests could justify the report's "READY" verdict. No -- added three more real scenarios, using these libraries' own real test patterns again:

  • test_deep_agent_parallel_subagents_via_graphtrace -- the real pattern from deepagents' own test_multiple_subagents_invoked_in_parallel: two different sub-agents invoked concurrently, each completing independently with a distinct result.
  • test_deep_agent_unknown_subagent_type_fails_gracefully_via_graphtrace -- a real safety property: delegating to an unregistered sub-agent type recovers gracefully, and the named sub-agent's own model genuinely never runs (checked against the fake model's own call history directly).
  • test_deep_agent_delegation_stays_within_latency_budget -- a real assert_budget check.

Both langgraph-swarm-py tests also tagged with real categories (handoff, tool_use) they'd been missing. The report's coverage breakdown across both real apps now reads six distinct categories, not three thin ones labeled once.

204 tests pass, full regression.

docs.title: Added (2026-10-27, same day) -- real test depth, round two: 7 real-app tests to 25
docs.text:
Asked again, more pointedly: "still only 7? can it be made of 30-50 cases?" Mined both libraries' own real test suites for scenarios not yet covered, rather than padding the existing two happy-path flows with reworded copies. Landed at 25 real-app tests, not 30-50 -- the honest ceiling of distinct, verified real material found, documented plainly rather than inflated to a round number.

  • tests/test_deepagents_filesystem_compat.py (new, 10 tests) -- deepagents' own built-in filesystem tools (write_file, edit_file, grep, ls, delete) through a full create_deep_agent() graph: write-then-edit (single and replace_all), graceful failure on a missing file/search string, grep across parallel-written files, ls-then-delete, and four real path-traversal/safety checks (../, a bare Windows absolute path, a ~-prefixed path, each severity="high").
  • tests/test_deepagents_permissions_todo_compat.py (new, 5 tests) -- FilesystemPermission write/delete enforcement and TodoListMiddleware, through a full agent conversation instead of deepagents' own unit-level internal-function tests. Includes the real all-or-nothing recursive-delete behavior from deepagents' own TestRecursiveDeletePermissions.
  • A second real structural gap, distinct from the nested-subgraph one found testing deepagents the first time: TodoListMiddleware's rejection of two parallel write_todos calls in one AIMessage (the real scenario from deepagents' own test_todo_middleware.py) happens inside wrap_tool_call, before graphtrace's patched BaseTool.invoke/ainvoke ever fires -- Trajectory.tool_calls is empty for both rejected calls even though the real conversation carries both real error ToolMessages. The agent's own behavior is unaffected; only the tool-call list undercounts in this one case. Documented with a real, verified assertion, not left as prose.
  • tests/test_langgraph_swarm_compat.py (3 new tests, 5 total) -- a three-agent handoff chain (Alice → Bob → Carol, confirming the subgraph index fix holds past two agents), a real tool exception (ZeroDivisionError) propagating through run_graph() with its exact type uncorrupted against a real external app's real tool for the first time, and state persisting across three conversation turns on the same checkpointer-backed thread.

222 tests pass, full regression. The report's coverage breakdown now spans ten real categories across two real external apps.

v0.1's full scope: the framework-agnostic Trajectory model and 12-function assertion API, the real LangGraph recording layer (including subgraphs), record/replay cassettes, a pinned-model judge contract with calibration, trace-to-test from a production export (Langfuse/OTel/LangSmith), a static HTML report, a real graphtrace CLI, and CI — 179 tests pass, full regression. Verified against real upstream sources throughout (a real live Groq model, the real openinference-semantic-conventions source, a real wheel build in a genuinely isolated clean venv), not just mocks and hand-built fixtures. Everything that follows, down to the next version header, was built and verified before this release.

docs.text:
• tests/test_judge_live.py: real integration tests against a live Groq model via litellm (the live-provider counterpart to test_judge.py's fakes), gated on GROQ_API_KEY. graphtrace.yaml, rubrics/refund_reply.yaml, evals/calibration.jsonl (a small, 4-case, hand-authored demonstration set -- not a statistically meaningful calibration) added to support it. 4 new tests.

Both confirmed to genuinely fail against the pre-fix recorder before being trusted as regression tests.
  • tests/test_importers.py: two new OTel tests for flattened chat-message reconstruction (see Fixed, below).
  • tests/test_codegen.py: a new test for list-of-messages LLM response normalization (see Fixed, below).
  • Real wheel build + twine check + a genuinely isolated clean-venv install, confirming report/templates/report.html.j2 is bundled and the console script / pytest11 entry point both work standalone -- the Week 4 packaging check.

docs.title: Fixed (2026-10-26) -- found by checking real sources, not by re-reading docs
docs.text:
• A real recorder bug: subgraph bookkeeping was global, single-namespace state. frameworks/langgraph/recorder.py's last_values/pending-task tracking was shared across every namespace. Harmless for a subgraph running alone (the outer graph's own next checkpoint always arrives later and corrects it before anything reads it again), but reproduced by hand: a subgraph running concurrently with another outer-level node (parallel fan-out) could commit that sibling's state_after early, using the subgraph's own unrelated partial state instead of the outer graph's. Fixed by scoping last_values/pending tasks/awaiting-commit list/committed-by-id per namespace -- a pure addition for the outer namespace (), which behaves identically to before (it's the only namespace that existed prior to subgraphs).
  • Step.kind's "subgraph_enter"/"subgraph_exit" were declared in the type (since Week 1) but never actually produced. Nothing in the recorder ever set a step's kind to either value -- a subgraph-wrapping node's own task/task_result pair looks identical in shape to an ordinary node's. Fixed: the recorder now detects a subgraph (a child event arriving at a namespace that extends a pending task's) and emits a subgraph_enter step immediately (so it appears before its children in the path) plus a subgraph_exit step when the wrapping task's own checkpoint finally arrives (necessarily last). The alternative -- collapsing the whole subgraph into one opaque step -- was considered and rejected: confirmed by hand that a call made inside a subgraph's own node is attributed to that inner node's task id, never the wrapper's, so collapsing it would have silently dropped those LLM/tool calls from the trajectory entirely.
  • importers/otel.py read an attribute key that can never exist in a real export. Fetched and quoted openinference-semantic-conventions's own source directly: there is no single "llm.input_messages" attribute -- chat messages are flattened per-index (llm.input_messages.0.message.content/.role, .1....). The old fallback silently never matched anything real, always falling through to input.value. Fixed with real per-index reconstruction (_flattened_messages()).
  • codegen/test_writer.py's _normalize_llm_response would have stringified a reconstructed message list wholesale ("[{'role': 'assistant', 'content': '...'}]") instead of extracting the actual reply text, the moment the otel importer fix above started producing that shape. Fixed to extract the last message's content, matching what a real AIMessage.content would hold.
  • .env.example documented a GRAPHTRACE_JUDGE_API_KEY variable that nothing in the codebase ever read. judge/client.py never reads an env var itself -- litellm.completion() resolves the real provider key (GROQ_API_KEY, etc.) straight from the environment, based on the model string's own prefix. Fixed to document the real, working pattern (mirroring kbguard's own .env.example).
  • A methodology bug caught mid-verification, not shipped: the first "clean venv" packaging check used source venv/Scripts/activate, which silently resolved python/pip to the system interpreter instead of the venv's own -- meaning it wasn't actually testing in isolation at all. Caught by checking sys.executable, not assumed correct; redone by invoking the venv's own python.exe directly.

docs.title: Changed (2026-10-26)
docs.text:
• core/trajectory.py's Step.index now documented honestly: it reflects when LangGraph started a step's task, not necessarily the step's final position in Trajectory.steps -- a subgraph's subgraph_exit step is created (and indexed) when its wrapping task starts, but only committed after every one of its children, since a subgraph's own completion genuinely can't be known before they are. No assert_* function keys off .index today, so this was a safe, additive clarification, not a behavior change needing a migration.
  • importers/langsmith.py and importers/langfuse.py's field-name assumptions independently re-confirmed against real upstream sources (the LangSmith SDK's own RunTree test file + the official run-data-format doc; the current GET /api/public/v2/observations API reference) rather than left as original, unverified guesses -- both held up as correct. Where LangSmith actually stores an llm run's model name genuinely isn't documented anywhere; confirmed as a real gap in LangSmith's own docs, not just a gap in this project's research, and left honestly flagged rather than guessed at.

docs.text:
• Project scaffold: pyproject.toml (packaging, dev/docs extras), .gitignore, LICENSE (Apache-2.0), NOTICE, README.md.
  • core/trajectory.py: LLMCall, ToolCall, Step, Trajectory dataclasses, plus derived properties (path, visits, tool_calls, llm_calls, final_message, cost_usd, latency_s, tokens_total). 7 tests.

This closes Week 1's goal.
