Expected first real use: the judge contract, Week 3.
  • Week 3 — judge, calibration, trace-to-test, report, CLI (2026-10-26). judge/rubric.py (strict pydantic Rubric/Criterion), judge/client.py (JudgeClient with litellm imported lazily inside ask_json() alone; grade() reuses replay/engine.resolve_call() directly, so a judge verdict is cached exactly like an LLM/tool call), judge/calibrate.py (per-criterion agreement/Cohen's kappa, never cached, always a real judge call). importers/base.py (NormalizedTrace/NormalizedSpan, TraceImporter protocol) plus importers/{langfuse,otel,langsmith}.py — none verified against a live export from a real account, each module's docstring states exactly what's confirmed vs. representative-but-unverified. codegen/test_writer.py (graphtrace from-trace — cassette + generated pytest file from a NormalizedTrace). report/results.py (TestResult, JSON-safe by construction), report/html.py + report/templates/report.html.j2 (Jinja2, autoescape=True, confirmed with a real XSS test). plugin.py extended with --gt-report=<path> (collects a TestResult per test via a pytest_runtest_makereport wrapper hook, renders the HTML report + a results.json at session end). cli.py + [project.scripts] (a real graphtrace console command: from-trace, calibrate, report). .github/workflows/graphtrace.yml (pytest + mkdocs build --strict, both confirmed green locally first). 66 new tests (tests/test_judge.py, tests/test_importers.py, tests/test_codegen.py, tests/test_report.py, tests/test_cli.py, plus tests/test_replay.py and tests/test_plugin.py growing). 169 tests pass total. This closes Week 3's goal — every "Planned" guide page for judge/calibration, trace-to-test, report/CI, and the CLI reference is now real, verified content.
  • Week 2 — record, replay, cassettes, config (2026-10-22). replay/cassette.py (YAML cassettes, ruamel.yaml round-trip mode, proven byte-identical on a load-then-save round trip), replay/matcher.py (node/kind/hash(request)/occurrence keys), replay/modes.py (resolve_mode()), replay/context.py (ReplayContext), replay/engine.py (resolve_call() — the generic record/replay decision tree, deliberately framework-agnostic: operates on plain YAML-safe data only, so a future CrewAI/AutoGen interceptor, v0.4, reuses it with zero changes). core/normalize.py (built-in timestamp/UUID stripping rules), core/budgets.py (Budgets.check(), the config-driven default-budget gate). config.py (graphtrace.yaml loading, pydantic, strict). 42 new tests (tests/test_replay.py, tests/test_mode_aware_interceptors.py, tests/test_config.py, plus tests/test_plugin.py growing from 2 to 6). 103 tests pass total, full regression, ~2 seconds — well inside the "20+ tests, under 30s" goal. Verified end to end against the real examples/refund_agent demo agent: recorded once, then replayed with the real BaseChatModel.invoke/BaseTool.invoke patched to raise if ever actually reached — zero real calls, proven by direct observation at the layer below graphtrace's own control.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Two corrections to the trace-to-test design, found only by actually trying to make a generated test replay-able against the real interceptor/engine layer, not by re-reading the architecture plan's description of it (2026-10-26):
  • replay/engine.py gained a position-only fallback match for codegen's cassettes. Every other cassette in this project matches a call by hashing its exact request — correct, because a real retry against the real graph reproduces the same request. An imported trace's own request field is whatever shape the source observability platform exported it in (Langfuse's JSON, an OTel attribute string, a LangSmith run's inputs), which structurally can never equal the real str(list[BaseMessage]) the live LangGraph interceptor hashes at replay time — there is no transformation between the two that would make exact-hash matching work here. Fixed by having codegen/test_writer.py write cassette entries with a literal any hash segment (node/kind/any/occurrence), and teaching resolve_call() to try that position-only key only after the exact-hash lookup has already missed — so it can never shadow a real entry from a normal record-mode cassette.
  • The generated test's assertion narrowed from assert_path (exact sequence) to assert_visited (each node, at least once). A trace importer only ever sees LLM/tool calls — a node that makes neither (a routing branch, a human-in-the-loop interrupt point) is invisible to every source platform's own export. Asserting the exact path from spans alone would therefore claim knowledge the trace never actually contained. Fixed before this ever generated a test that could silently fail on a perfectly correct run; assert_path/assert_tool_calls_match are suggested in the generated TODO for once the real path is known.
  • codegen/test_writer.py's generated graph = factory() call now inspects the real target's signature first. A LangGraph builder function commonly takes a chat model (or other required config) as an argument — this project's own build_refund_graph(chat_model, ...) is written exactly that way — so assuming every factory is zero-argument would silently generate a wrong call for a genuinely common, not edge-case, shape. from-trace now imports --target for real and checks for any required parameter, emitting a # TODO: construct it the way your app really does placeholder instead of guessing when one exists (or when the import itself fails).
  • Three corrections to the recording design, found only by running real code against real langgraph/langchain-core (1.2 / 1.6), not by re-reading the architecture plan's description of them:
  • Call attribution moved off contextvars entirely. The original design tracked "the current node" with a ContextVar set by the recorder and read back by the interceptors. Confirmed by hand with a threading.current_thread() probe inside a parallel ("fan-out") node: LangGraph's Pregel engine runs node functions — including parallel ones — on a ThreadPoolExecutor worker thread, and ThreadPoolExecutor.submit() doesn't propagate the calling thread's contextvars into the worker by default. A ContextVar set while consuming graph.stream() in the main thread reads back empty inside the node that's supposed to see it. Replaced with config["metadata"]["langgraph_checkpoint_ns"] — a "{node_name}:{task_id}" string LangGraph itself attaches to every LLM/tool call, confirmed by hand to be byte-for-byte the same id the debug event stream uses for that task, including across repeated visits to the same node in a retry loop. This correlation key travels with the call itself through whatever thread actually executes it — strictly more robust than the ContextVar design even if threading had cooperated.
  • Chat-model patch target moved from _generate/_agenerate to invoke/ainvoke. Confirmed by hand ('_generate' in GenericFakeChatModel.__dict__ is True) that every concrete chat model — OpenAI's, Anthropic's, and LangChain's own GenericFakeChatModel — defines its own _generate, overriding BaseChatModel's. Patching the base class's _generate therefore patches a method real calls never resolve to; Python's method resolution finds the subclass's own override first, every time. invoke/ainvoke are never overridden by a concrete subclass (confirmed the same way) and carry the same config["metadata"] correlation key straight through — the same reasoning that already applied to tools (BaseTool.invoke, confirmed to be what LangGraph's real ToolNode actually calls, by reading its source, not _run).
  • stream_mode reduced from ["debug", "updates"] to ["debug"] alone. Checked both side by side against a real run: "updates"'s per-node payload is exactly task_result.result already, under a different key. Subscribing to it bought nothing.
  • recorder.py gained a flush() step and resume-deduplication beyond the original design: a step that pauses on an interrupt right after its task_result never gets a settling checkpoint event (confirmed by hand: the real debug-event stream for a paused run simply ends there) — flush() commits it anyway, using the graph's current get_state(config).values. Resuming re-runs that same node from the top under the same task id (confirmed by hand), so without dedup, the interrupted attempt's incomplete step would sit alongside the resumed, complete one as a duplicate; the recorder now replaces it instead.
  • plugin.py's scope reduced from the original plan: only the run_graph fixture is built. --gt-mode and the cassette/judge fixtures aren't added yet — they would do nothing today, and this project's own stated rule (docs/project/contributing.md) is not to ship a flag or fixture that doesn't actually do anything yet.

docs.title: Fixed (caught before any of this shipped, not after)
docs.text: • A real bug in the demo agent itself, caught by its own test suite doing exactly its job: examples/refund_agent's refund node unconditionally set refunded: True regardless of whether the human approved the request — a missing conditional edge after human_approval. test_refund_flow_rejected_by_human_does_not_refund failed against the original graph, exactly as it should have; fixed by routing human_approval to refund or give_up based on approved, not by weakening the test.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Project renamed graphcheck → graphtrace (2026-10-18). graphcheck is already published on PyPI as an unrelated Neo4j graph-data-quality tool — close enough in name and domain ("graph" + "check") to cause real confusion, and it would have blocked pip install graphcheck for this project entirely. Confirmed the collision via PyPI's simple index before renaming, and confirmed graphtrace was unclaimed on both PyPI and GitHub before committing to it. Renamed everything in one pass, not left half-done: the package (src/graphtrace/), every import, CLI flag names (--gc-mode → --gt-mode, etc.), the env var (GRAPHCHECK_MODE → GRAPHTRACE_MODE), the config filename (graphcheck.yaml → graphtrace.yaml), the internal plan doc, LICENSE/NOTICE/README.md, and the top-level folder itself (D:\GraphCheck → D:\GraphTrace).
  • Trajectory.cost_usd changed from "sums tokens via a runtime/pricing.py lookup" (the original architecture plan's implied design) to "sums a cost_usd field already set per LLMCall." The original design would have made core import from runtime, which breaks this project's own layering rule (core must never depend on runtime) — the field-based approach keeps core genuinely pricing- and framework-ignorant. See Core concepts: where cost comes from.
  • assert_retries' original architecture-plan example used a node name ("tool_call") that didn't exist anywhere in the plan's own running example graph, and the function's semantics versus assert_visits were never actually specified. Fixed by giving it a concrete, narrower meaning — "re-entered after one of its own tool calls errored" — and a real example using an actual node name. See Assertions: assert_retries.
  • assert_path's ... gap matching scoped down from "however many gaps the syntax could technically support" to exactly one, with a second gap raising ValueError rather than silently picking an interpretation. See Assertions: assert_path.
  • Three features adopted from validated prior art, tagged and scoped (2026-10-21) — a competitive-landscape review turned up real, evidenced tools worth copying rather than avoiding: assert_tool_calls_match (strict/unordered/subset/superset modes, straight from langchain-ai/agentevals, the official LangGraph ecosystem's own trajectory-match evaluator) built and tested the same day — 6 new tests, 37 total. Matches by tool name only, not args, a deliberate scope decision (agentevals treats sequence-matching and arg-matching as separate concerns; assert_tool_called(..., args_match=...) already covers the arg side). Cut-point replay (replay a recorded incident up to where it broke, then run a fix live from there, reusing the existing cassette-matching key unmodified — adopted from Chronicle, Microsoft, arXiv 2609.20625, whose own mutation-testing study is the evidence this is worth adopting) and statistical live-mode verification (a Wilson-interval Pass/Fail/Inconclusive verdict across N real trials instead of trusting one flaky nightly run — adopted from AgentAssay, arXiv 2603.02601) are both tagged v0.2, bundled with the already-planned security/observability work since all four build on the same shipped core. See Cut-point replay, Assertions: assert_tool_calls_match, and Recording & replay: statistical live-mode verification.
  • CrewAI/AutoGen support planned and tagged v0.4 (2026-10-21). Previously an untagged, undesigned aspiration in the plan's non-goals list ("these can come later," no version, no design section) — now a real phase with a design (concept-mapping table, per-framework interceptor decision, one open question flagged rather than guessed) in the internal plan doc §20, and a file-by-file build plan. One architecture change made proactively in v0.1 itself as a result: the planned runtime/ package was never built, so it's replaced before Week 1's recorder/runner land with frameworks/base.py (a FrameworkRunner Protocol) + frameworks/langgraph/ (v0.1's only implementation) — meaning v0.4's frameworks/crewai//frameworks/autogen/ will be new packages, not a refactor of a shipped one. Config/CLI renamed ahead of need to match: graph: → target: (+ new framework: field), --graph → --target. See Multi-framework support.
  • The cassette format's args/result fields (tool-specific, per the original plan's sketch) became request/response — one consistent shape across both kind: llm and kind: tool entries turned out simpler than two different ones, and reads naturally either way ("the request", "the response").
  • plugin.py grew real functional scope beyond Week 1's deliberately-reduced version: --gt-mode (pytest_addoption), the run_graph fixture's cassette directory now comes from graphtrace.yaml, and the fixture auto-applies budgets.default after every call.

docs.title: Fixed (caught before any of this shipped, not after)
docs.text:
• The architecture plan's component diagram was missing the codegen/test-writer node and the judge→cassette caching link that the plan's own prose (trace-to-test, judge contract) already described — fixed in the plan doc so the diagram and the text agree.
  • The plan's cassette tech-stack choice listed "PyYAML / ruamel.yaml" as if interchangeable — plain PyYAML's default dump doesn't actually guarantee the stable key order the plan's own goal ("cassettes diff well in PRs") depends on. Pinned to ruamel.yaml round-trip mode.
  • The plan's trace-to-test section didn't say what happens to a human-in-the-loop interrupt on import — a resume value isn't recoverable from a trace. Fixed by specifying a # TODO stub instead of a guessed value, documented on Trace-to-test.
  • ruamel.yaml's round-trip mode breaking a replayed value, found running real tests, not anticipated by any prior design pass: a loaded float comes back as a ScalarFloat subclass (preserving its exact on-disk formatting, exactly what makes the cassette round-trip-identity guarantee true) — which then made LangGraph's own checkpointer raise TypeError: Type is not msgpack serializable: ScalarFloat the moment that value flowed into a replayed tool result and got persisted as graph state. Fixed with replay/cassette.to_plain_python(), applied only to a value about to flow back into real code, never to a value still destined for the cassette file — keeping both guarantees true at once instead of trading one for the other.
  • An early draft of the replay error path re-raised every tool error (live or replayed) as a generic RuntimeError, which would have silently broken any node whose own except SomeSpecificError: depends on the real exception type — confirmed this would have broken Week 1's own test_run_graph_tool_call_error_is_captured_without_crashing_when_node_catches_it before it ever shipped. Fixed so only a replayed failure (genuinely unrecoverable type info once serialized to YAML) becomes a generic RuntimeError; a live exception always keeps its exact type via a bare raise.

docs.title: Design decisions locked in
docs.text:
• core/ (data model + assertions) has zero dependencies on LangGraph, an LLM SDK, or graphtrace.frameworks — enforced by convention today (no lint rule yet; see Contributing).
  • Framework-specific interception is not shared across frameworks, even though the FrameworkRunner Protocol and Trajectory output are. CrewAI and AutoGen don't reliably call through the same LangChain classes graphtrace's LangGraph interceptor patches, so each frameworks/<name>/interceptors.py targets that framework's own real call surface rather than assuming one patch covers all three.
  • AutoGen's dynamic speaker selection vs. assert_path's exact-match/single-gap model is an explicitly open question for v0.4, not assumed solved — see graphtrace.md §20.5. Documenting a gap honestly beats guessing an answer now and correcting it later.
  • TrajectoryAssertionError subclasses AssertionError, not Exception — so a bare assert and an assert_path(...) failure look the same to pytest and to pytest.raises(AssertionError).
  • assert_state_at's occurrence parameter follows Python list-indexing (-1 = most recent visit, 0 = first) rather than inventing a new convention.
  • any_str() is the only matcher built — more are added when a real test needs one, not speculatively.
  • Licensing: Apache-2.0, single license, no feature gating, plus a lightweight CLA policy — decided before any commercial scope existed, so it never has to be partially undone later. See the project's internal plan doc, section 17.
  • replay/engine.py's resolve_call() never imports LangChain or LangGraph, and never sees an AIMessage/ToolMessage object — only plain dicts/strings/numbers. All LangChain-specific serialization lives in frameworks/langgraph/interceptors.py, on either side of the call into resolve_call(). This is the actual test of whether record/replay stays reusable for v0.4's CrewAI/AutoGen interceptors, not just an aspiration.
  • Redaction (graphtrace.yaml's replay.redact) is validated but deliberately not enforced yet — shipping a config field that looks like it protects secrets before it actually does would be worse than not having the field at all. Documented as an open gap everywhere it's relevant (docs/guide/recording-and-replay.md, docs/guide/configuration.md), not silently assumed.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: graphtrace's v0.1 scope is complete — see Roadmap & status for exactly what's built, including every real bug found and fixed along the way. v0.2 (security test pack, observability export, cut-point replay, statistical live-mode verification) and v0.4 (CrewAI/AutoGen support) are designed but not started; check the roadmap before picking either up.

docs.title: Development setup
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/devbyanoop/graphtrace.git
cd graphtrace
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # or .venv/Scripts/activate on Windows (Git Bash)
pip install -e ".[dev]"

Copy .env.example to .env and fill in a real provider key if you want tests/test_judge_live.py's 4 live tests to run too (they skip cleanly without one).

docs.title: Running checks locally
docs.text:
pytest                      # 222 tests, full regression
mkdocs build --strict       # this docs site, strict mode (pip install -e ".[docs]" first)

Both are what .github/workflows/graphtrace.yml runs on every push/PR. Linting (ruff) and strict type-checking (mypy) aren't configured yet — src/graphtrace/py.typed (PEP 561) is already in place for an external type-checker to use against this package, but nothing in this repo enforces it internally yet. If you add either, wire it into this page and into CI in the same change, not as a follow-up.

docs.title: Design rules that apply to every change
docs.text:
1. core/ never imports LangGraph, an LLM SDK, or anything from frameworks//replay//judge//importers/. A Trajectory is plain dataclasses and plain Python values — see Core concepts.
  2. replay/engine.py never imports LangChain or LangGraph, and never sees a framework object — only plain dicts/strings/numbers in and out. All framework-specific serialization lives in frameworks/<name>/interceptors.py, on either side of the call into resolve_call(). This is what keeps record/replay reusable for v0.4's CrewAI/AutoGen interceptors without rewriting it.
  3. A deliberate scope decision gets documented, not silently shipped. assert_path's single-gap limit, the trace-to-test generated assertion being assert_visited rather than assert_path, and the judge's scale: "1-5" validating-but-not-scoring are all written down on their own guide page and in the changelog — a reviewer (or future you) shouldn't have to reverse-engineer why from the diff alone.
  4. No invented numbers. Cost and token budgets come from real recorded usage (LLMCall.cost_usd, .prompt_tokens/.completion_tokens), never an estimate computed on the fly. Judge agreement comes from a real calibration run, never a guessed kappa.
  5. Verify a fast-moving library's real behavior by running real code before trusting a design doc's description of it — this project's single most repeated lesson (see the roadmap's build history): contextvars attribution, the _generate patch target, ruamel.yaml's ScalarFloat, Cohen's kappa for a systematic label flip, and subgraph state bookkeeping were all confirmed wrong this way, not by re-reading a plan that looked reasonable on paper.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
This guide (docs/) is written incrementally, alongside the code — a feature's documentation is written and verified the same day the feature itself is built and tested, not ahead of time. A page for a genuinely unbuilt feature (v0.2/v0.4 scope) carries an explicit "Planned" warning with scope only, no invented usage examples. If you're adding a feature, update its doc page in the same change.

Preview the docs site locally:

pip install -e ".[docs]"
mkdocs serve

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: This page grows as real questions come in. It starts with a few that are already answerable from design decisions made so far.

docs.title: Will graphtrace ever call a real LLM or tool during a CI run?
docs.text: Only if you set mode="live" or configure --gt-mode=live. The intended default for CI is replay mode: responses come from a cassette on disk (or, for an imported production trace, from graphtrace from-trace's own generated cassette), and the real LLM/tool are never reached — confirmed by patching the real underlying BaseChatModel.invoke/BaseTool.invoke to raise if they're ever actually reached, not just by trusting the replay logic's own reasoning. live mode is meant for a separate, nightly drift check, not the default PR gate.

docs.title: Does the judge ever get cached the same way?
docs.text: Yes — grade() reuses the exact same resolve_call() cassette machinery an LLM/tool call goes through, keyed by (rubric.id, "judge", request). A replay-mode test run never calls the judge, confirmed against a real recorded cassette and a real Groq model, not just a fake one. See Judge & calibration.

docs.title: Why does core refuse to import anything LangGraph-related?
docs.text: So everything built on top of a Trajectory — assertions, budgets, the HTML report — stays reusable no matter what produced that Trajectory. See Core concepts: why core stays framework-agnostic.

docs.title: Why does assert_path only support one ... gap?
docs.text: Supporting several, non-overlapping gaps is possible, but makes failure messages genuinely ambiguous ("which gap swallowed the mismatch?"), and nothing in the project's own goals needs it yet. See Assertions: assert_path.

docs.title: Why does a generated test from graphtrace from-trace assert assert_visited, not assert_path?
docs.text: Because a trace importer only ever sees LLM/tool calls — a node that makes neither (a routing branch, a human-in-the-loop interrupt point) is invisible to every source platform's own export. Claiming to assert the exact path from spans alone would be a false promise, not a reasonable approximation. See Trace-to-test.

docs.title: How is assert_retries different from assert_visits?
docs.text: assert_visits just counts how many times a node ran — fine for a node that's a normal loop body. assert_retries counts only re-entries that happened after that node's own tool call failed — an actual retry, not a designed loop. See Assertions: assert_retries.

docs.title: Does graphtrace handle subgraphs (a node whose value is itself a compiled graph)?
docs.text: Yes, transparently — the subgraph's own inner nodes show up as their own steps (so a real LLM/tool call made inside one is never lost), bracketed by subgraph_enter/subgraph_exit steps marking the boundary. This needed a real bug fix to get right: see Recording & replay for the full account.

docs.title: Will graphtrace ever support CrewAI or AutoGen?
docs.text: Yes, planned for v0.4 (gated on v0.1 shipping first) — see Multi-framework support. That's a real, designed phase, not an open-ended "maybe someday": the core data model needs zero changes (see the previous question), and the one real architecture decision this needs — splitting the LangGraph-specific layer into frameworks/base.py (a shared contract) + frameworks/langgraph/ — was already built that way in v0.1, specifically so v0.4 is a new package, not a rename of a shipped one.

docs.title: Why does graphtrace borrow designs from other tools instead of inventing its own?
docs.text: Because a validated idea is worth more than a novel one. assert_tool_calls_match's four modes come straight from langchain-ai/agentevals (the official LangGraph ecosystem's own answer, already adopted widely); cut-point replay comes from a Microsoft research paper (Chronicle, arXiv 2609.20625) with a mutation-testing study backing it; the statistical live-mode verdict comes from another published paper (AgentAssay, arXiv 2603.02601, see Recording & replay). Reinventing any of these from scratch, worse, to avoid "just copying," would be a worse outcome for anyone actually using graphtrace. See Roadmap & status for where each one stands today.

docs.title: Something's missing from this FAQ
docs.text: Open an issue, or see Contributing.

docs.title: Roadmap & status
docs.text:
This page is the single source of truth for "is X actually built yet?" — updated the same day any item's status changes, not retroactively. If a page elsewhere in this guide seems to claim more than this page shows as done, trust this page.

Last updated: 2026-10-26

docs.title: Phase 0 — scaffold
docs.text:
• [x] Git repository, .gitignore
  • [x] pyproject.toml — packaging, dev/docs extras
  • [x] Python virtual environment, editable install verified
  • [x] LICENSE (Apache-2.0) + NOTICE
  • [x] This documentation site (MkDocs + Material)

Rename note: the project was originally named graphcheck. Renamed to graphtrace on 2026-10-18 — graphcheck collides on PyPI with an unrelated, actively-published Neo4j graph-data-quality tool of the same name, confirmed before anything of this project went public. Package, imports, CLI flag names (--gt-mode, --gt-report, --gt-export), env var (GRAPHTRACE_MODE), config filename (graphtrace.yaml), the internal plan doc, and the top-level folder were all updated together in one pass, not left half-renamed.

docs.title: Week 1 — foundations
docs.text:
Goal (per the build plan): plugin entry point, Trajectory, recorder, run_graph, core assertions, demo agent — 10 tests on a demo agent passing in live mode.

Status: met (2026-10-22). Both halves are done and verified: the framework-agnostic data model/assertion API, and the LangGraph-specific recorder/runner/interceptors/plugin/demo agent.

  • [x] core/trajectory.py — LLMCall, ToolCall, Step, Trajectory dataclasses plus derived properties (path, visits, tool_calls, llm_calls, final_message, cost_usd, latency_s, tokens_total). Deliberate fix versus the original architecture plan: cost_usd is a field precomputed per LLMCall, not something Trajectory computes by reaching into a pricing table — the original plan would have made core depend on the LangGraph-specific layer, breaking the project's own layering rule. 7 tests, see Core concepts.
  • [x] core/errors.py — TrajectoryAssertionError (subclasses AssertionError so pytest.raises(AssertionError) still catches it) plus an index-by-index path diff formatter, so a path mismatch reads as a diff, not two dumped lists.
  • [x] core/matchers.py — any_str(), the one matcher the architecture plan actually names; a Matcher base class ready for more the day a real test needs one.
  • [x] core/assertions.py — all 12 assert_* functions. Two deliberate scope decisions versus the original plan, both documented on Assertions: assert_path's ... gap supports exactly one gap (a second raises ValueError rather than guessing which gap a mismatch belongs to), and assert_retries specifically means "a node re-entered after one of its own tool calls errored," not just "visited more than once" — distinct from assert_visits. The 12th, assert_tool_calls_match, is adopted deliberately from langchain-ai/agentevals' own trajectory-match evaluator (strict/unordered/subset/superset modes) rather than invented. 30 tests.
  • [x] frameworks/base.py — the FrameworkRunner Protocol, built before the LangGraph implementation below. Added to the plan on 2026-10-21 specifically so v0.4's CrewAI/AutoGen support (see Multi-framework support) is a new package later, not a refactor of a shipped one. src/graphtrace/py.typed added alongside it (PEP 561 marker, so the Protocol type-checks for an external implementer) — proactively, since this project has no mypy wired up yet to actually confirm the Protocol is satisfied correctly; see Contributing.
  • [x] frameworks/pricing.py — token → USD table, sets LLMCall.cost_usd at record time.
  • [x] frameworks/langgraph/interceptors.py — patches BaseChatModel.invoke/ainvoke and BaseTool.invoke/ainvoke. Corrected from the original plan's _generate/_run: every concrete chat model (OpenAI's, Anthropic's, LangChain's own GenericFakeChatModel) overrides _generate itself, so patching the base class's version intercepts nothing real — confirmed by hand before trusting it. Attribution uses config["metadata"]["langgraph_checkpoint_ns"] (a "{node}:{task_id}" string LangGraph itself attaches), not the originally-planned contextvars — a ContextVar set while consuming the event stream doesn't survive into the ThreadPoolExecutor worker thread LangGraph actually runs parallel nodes on, confirmed with a threading.current_thread() probe before relying on it.
  • [x] frameworks/langgraph/recorder.py — turns LangGraph's debug stream into Steps (subscribing to debug alone; updates turned out to duplicate task_result.result exactly). Added a flush() step and resume-dedup logic beyond the original design: a step paused on an interrupt never gets a settling checkpoint event, and resuming re-runs it under the same task id, which would otherwise show up as a duplicate.
  • [x] frameworks/langgraph/runner.py — run_graph() and arun_graph().
  • [x] plugin.py — pytest entry point (pytest11), run_graph fixture. Scope reduced from the original plan: --gt-mode and the cassette/judge fixtures aren't added yet since they'd do nothing today.
  • [x] examples/refund_agent/ — a demo agent to record and assert against for real. Writing its tests caught a real bug in the agent itself: refund unconditionally refunded regardless of whether the human approved, a missing conditional edge.

docs.title: Week 2 — record, replay, cassettes, config
docs.text:
Goal (per the build plan): 20+ tests pass offline (no real LLM/tool calls) in under 30 seconds.

Status: met (2026-10-22).

  • [x] replay/cassette.py — YAML cassettes via ruamel.yaml round-trip mode, proven byte-identical on a load-then-save round trip. Real bug found along the way: round-trip mode wraps a loaded float in a ScalarFloat subclass (to preserve exact formatting), which then broke a replayed tool result the moment it flowed into LangGraph's own state and got msgpack-serialized by its checkpointer. Fixed with to_plain_python(), applied only when a value is about to flow back into real code, never on a value still destined for the cassette file.
  • [x] replay/matcher.py — node/kind/hash(request)/occurrence keys; two identical requests from the same node (a retry) match their own two recorded entries in order.
  • [x] replay/modes.py, replay/context.py, replay/engine.py — resolve_call(), the generic record/replay decision tree, kept framework-agnostic (plain YAML-safe data in and out) so a future CrewAI/AutoGen interceptor (v0.4) reuses it unmodified.
  • [x] frameworks/langgraph/interceptors.py/runner.py made mode-aware. Verified by recording the Week 1 demo agent once, then replaying it with the real underlying BaseChatModel.invoke/BaseTool.invoke patched to raise if ever actually reached — zero real calls, proven by direct observation, not inferred from the replay logic's own correctness.
  • [x] core/normalize.py (the built-in timestamp/UUID rules), core/budgets.py (the config-driven default-budget check).
  • [x] config.py — graphtrace.yaml loading, pydantic, strict. framework: crewai (not valid until v0.4) is rejected at load time, not just documented as unsupported.
  • [x] plugin.py extended: --gt-mode CLI flag, cassette directory from config, and the run_graph fixture now auto-applies budgets.default after every call — a test that never calls assert_budget(...) itself still fails if the configured default is exceeded.

103 tests pass today (pytest from a clean pip install -e ".[dev]") — full regression, every file, in about 2 seconds. See Installation to verify this yourself.

docs.title: Week 3 — judge, trace-to-test, report, CLI
docs.text:
Goal (per the build plan): the judge contract and calibration, trace importers (Langfuse/OTel/LangSmith), codegen/test_writer.py, the HTML report, and a real graphtrace CLI — flipping every "Planned" guide page above from aspiration to real, verified behaviour.

Status: met (2026-10-26).

  • [x] judge/rubric.py, judge/client.py — strict pydantic Rubric/Criterion, JudgeClient (litellm imported lazily, inside ask_json() alone — constructing a client or hitting a cassette-replayed verdict never needs it installed), grade() reusing replay/engine.resolve_call() directly so a judge verdict is cached exactly like an LLM/tool call.
  • [x] judge/calibrate.py — per-criterion agreement and Cohen's kappa against a human-labelled calibration set. Real correction found by checking the math by hand: this project's own build plan originally claimed "full disagreement scores kappa 0.0" — false for balanced labels; a perfect inversion actually scores -1.0 (real anti-correlation, worse than chance), confirmed against both the hand-derived formula and the real installed sklearn. See Judge & calibration for the corrected explanation.
  • [x] importers/base.py, importers/{langfuse,otel,langsmith}.py — one shared NormalizedTrace/NormalizedSpan shape, one small TraceImporter protocol per source. None of the three are verified against a live export from a real account (no account access) — each module's own docstring says exactly what's confirmed vs. representative-but-unverified, rather than overclaiming.
  • [x] codegen/test_writer.py — graphtrace from-trace. Two real design gaps found and fixed while building this, not assumed away:
    1. An imported trace's request field can never hash-match the real str(list[BaseMessage]) the live LangGraph interceptor hashes at replay time (different platforms serialize completely differently) — replay/engine.py gained a position-only fallback match (node/kind/any/occurrence), scoped so it can never shadow a real recorded cassette entry.
    2. A generated test originally asserted the exact path (assert_path) from the trace's spans — but spans only capture LLM/tool calls, so a node that makes neither (a routing branch, an interrupt point) is invisible to every importer. Asserting an exact path from that would be a false promise; the generated test now asserts assert_visited per node that made a captured call instead, with a TODO pointing at assert_path/assert_tool_calls_match for tightening it by hand. Also: a factory requiring arguments (this project's own build_refund_graph(chat_model, ...) is written exactly that way) is now detected by actually importing --target and inspecting its signature, rather than assuming every factory is zero-argument.
  • [x] report/results.py, report/html.py — TestResult (JSON-safe by construction), Jinja2 autoescape=True (confirmed with a real XSS test: trajectory state containing <script> renders escaped). Verified against a real run_graph() Trajectory from the Week 1 demo agent, not just a hand-built one.
  • [x] plugin.py extended: --gt-report=<path> collects a TestResult per test (including a distinct "error" outcome for a test whose fixture failed before the body ran) and renders the HTML report — plus a results.json alongside it — at session end.
  • [x] cli.py, [project.scripts] — a real graphtrace console command: from-trace, calibrate, report. The actual verify-by: a real Langfuse-shaped trace fixture, run through graphtrace from-trace for real, produces a generated test file that a real pytest --gt-mode=replay subprocess run then passes — checked end to end, not just that generate_test() returns some string.
  • [x] .github/workflows/graphtrace.yml — pytest + mkdocs build --strict on every push/PR, both confirmed green locally before committing to the claim.

169 tests pass today, full regression. See Judge & calibration, Trace-to-test, Report & CI, and the CLI reference.

docs.title: Real-world readiness hardening (2026-10-26)
docs.text:
Not a new build-plan week — a deliberate pass asking "is this actually ready to validate against a real application?" and closing every gap the honest answer surfaced, rather than letting "169 tests pass" stand in for real-world readiness. 178 tests pass after this pass, full regression (~30s with the live Groq tests included, ~25s without — see below).

  • The judge, verified against a real provider for the first time. GROQ_API_KEY (real, working) + a real graphtrace.yaml/rubrics/refund_reply.yaml/evals/calibration.jsonl (a small, 4-case, hand-authored demonstration set, honestly not the 20-50 cases a production threshold needs). tests/test_judge_live.py (4 tests, skips cleanly without the key, same pattern as kbguard's live Pinecone test) proves grade()/calibrate() work against a real groq/openai/gpt-oss-120b model, including that a replayed cassette genuinely never calls the judge again — the fake-litellm tests already covered the shape of this; this covers whether it's actually true.
  • A real, previously-undetected recorder bug: subgraphs. Step.kind's "subgraph_enter"/"subgraph_exit" existed in the type since Week 1 but were never actually produced — nothing tested a node whose value is itself a compiled graph. Investigated by hand against a real nested graph (confirmed: a subgraph's own inner checkpoints are tagged with a deeper namespace, and chain langgraph_checkpoint_ns correctly, so LLM/tool-call attribution already worked). What didn't: the recorder's last_values/pending-task bookkeeping was global, single-namespace state, so a subgraph running concurrently with another outer-level node could have the sibling's state_after committed early using the subgraph's own unrelated partial state — reproduced by hand, then fixed by scoping that bookkeeping per namespace, and by actually emitting subgraph_enter/subgraph_exit (transparently exposing the subgraph's own inner nodes, rather than collapsing it to one step and silently losing their LLM/tool calls). Both failure modes are now regression tests in tests/test_runner.py, each confirmed to genuinely fail against the pre-fix code before trusting them.
  • Packaging, actually checked this time. A real wheel build (python -m build), twine check (passed), and inspection confirmed report/templates/report.html.j2 is bundled by hatchling's default rules — the Week 4 concern noted here previously turned out to be a non-issue, but only checking it that way earns believing it. Installed into a venv with its own python.exe invoked directly (the first attempt used source .../activate, which silently resolved to the system Python instead of the venv's — caught before it invalidated the test) and confirmed the console script, python -m graphtrace.cli, and the pytest11 entry point all work from a wheel-only install with nothing else on the path.
  • Trace importers, checked against real upstream sources, not just documentation summaries. Fetched and quoted the real openinference-semantic-conventions source directly: found that llm.input_messages/llm.output_messages are never literal attribute keys at all (messages are flattened per-index, llm.input_messages.0.message.content/.role) — importers/otel.py's old fallback read a key that could never match anything in a real export, silently falling through to input.value every time. Fixed with real per-index reconstruction, which surfaced a second bug one level up: codegen/test_writer.py's _normalize_llm_response would have stringified that reconstructed message list wholesale ("[{'role': ...}]") instead of extracting the actual reply text — fixed to extract the last message's content, the way a real AIMessage.content would read. importers/langsmith.py's field names (run_type/inputs/outputs/start_time/end_time/name) were independently re-confirmed against the real SDK's own RunTree test file and the official run-data-format doc; where the model name actually lives for an llm run genuinely isn't documented anywhere (confirmed by checking, not just not-knowing) and stays an honestly-flagged gap. importers/langfuse.py's observation field names were independently re-confirmed against the real, current GET /api/public/v2/observations API reference. None of the three importers have still been run against a live account export -- that specific gap needs real account access, which checking public API docs and SDK source can't substitute for.

docs.title: Week 4 — done (2026-10-26). v0.1 is release-ready.
docs.text:
PyPI packaging check was already done above (moved into the hardening pass, since it needed doing before any "ready for real apps" claim meant anything). This pass closed the rest:

  • README + full docs sweep. docs/index.md was still describing "early development" with recording/replay marked "planned" in its own diagram, years after it shipped; installation.md/quickstart.md still had Week-1-era test counts and a cassette="unused" comment claiming record/replay "doesn't exist yet"; recording-and-replay.md still said subgraphs were "not yet tested," after they'd already been found broken and fixed in the hardening pass above; configuration.md still said judge/report config "isn't consulted by anything yet," after the CLI had been consulting both for days. All corrected.
  • A real sample trace-to-test: examples/sample_trace/ — a Langfuse-shaped export with a real retry, run through the real CLI (graphtrace from-trace), producing a generated test confirmed passing unedited.
  • A real sample HTML report: examples/sample_report/ — two real passing trajectories, one real judge verdict against a live Groq model, and one deliberate real failure, so the report shows what every state actually looks like. Building it surfaced one more real gap: graphtrace report had no --title option, so a previous render couldn't be reproduced byte-for-byte from its own results.json — fixed, confirmed with a real diff. Also surfaced a test-isolation gap: a bare pytest from the repo root was silently sweeping examples/sample_trace/'s own checked-in generated test into the main suite's count — fixed with testpaths = ["tests"] in pyproject.toml.
  • A write-up for outreach: Case study — the five real bugs found across this whole build, written for an external reader deciding whether to hire the person who found them, not as internal notes.
  • changelog.md: [Unreleased] renamed to [0.1.0] - 2026-10-26, with a fresh, empty [Unreleased] above it.

179 tests pass today, full regression. Not yet actually tagged or published anywhere (PyPI, GitHub) — that's a separate decision for whoever owns this repository to make, not implied by "release-ready." Redaction and custom normalize rules (both part of Week 2's original scope) are still not built — see Recording & replay for that specific, still-open gap.

docs.title: Real-world validation: a real external app (2026-10-26, same day)
docs.text:
Everything above was verified against this project's own demo agent, hand-written specifically to exercise graphtrace's own features. This pass pointed run_graph() at a real, official, external app instead — langchain-ai/langgraph-swarm-py (the LangGraph team's own multi-agent swarm library, MIT, ~1.6k stars) — and found three more real bugs, none of which the demo agent had ever been capable of exercising. tests/test_langgraph_swarm_compat.py keeps this as a permanent, real (not hand-approximated) regression test, gated behind the dev extra's new langgraph-swarm dependency with pytest.importorskip.

  1. LangChain 1.x's create_agent() doesn't thread an explicit config into its model call. Confirmed by hand that BaseChatModel.invoke() receives config=None every time under this newer agent abstraction — every call was attributed to node "?" instead of the real node name, because the explicit-config lookup this project's interceptors relied on since Week 1 simply had nothing to read. The real metadata was still there, just reachable only through LangChain's own ambient, contextvar-based config propagation (langchain_core.runnables.config). Fixed by resolving metadata through ensure_config(config) (the same public function LangChain's own runnables use for exactly this fallback) instead of reading config directly — what's forwarded to the real underlying call is untouched either way.
  2. A subgraph's subgraph_enter/subgraph_exit step pair had their index values backwards. Yesterday's subgraph fix created a new step for the enter marker with a fresh (later) index, while the exit marker kept the parent's original (earlier) one — exit showing a lower number than its own enter. Fixed by swapping which step plays which role: the parent's original, early-indexed step becomes the enter marker; a new step, indexed at detection time (always later), becomes the eventual exit.
  3. A tool call returning Command(graph=Command.PARENT, ...) — LangGraph's own real handoff mechanism — never gets its own task_result/checkpoint event at all. Confirmed against the real debug-event stream: the child task's completion folds directly into the parent's own task_result, with no settling point for the child in between. Without a fix, that step would simply never commit — not even via flush()'s existing "no checkpoint is ever coming" fallback, since a different event (the parent's own resolution) is what actually signals it's over. Fixed by absorbing any task still pending directly under a resolving task's own namespace the instant that happens. A closely related second bug surfaced at the same time: neither the tool's real args (which can carry an entire injected graph state, including raw BaseMessage objects — LangGraph's own "inject full state as a tool arg" pattern) nor a real Command result were YAML-safe, crashing cassette writes outright. Fixed with a generic, recursive serializer (_yaml_safe/_restore_value) that round-trips BaseMessage (human/ai/tool/system) and Command correctly through replay — not just avoiding a crash, but handing back a real Command object on replay, since a real node's own isinstance(result, Command) check would otherwise silently fail against a plain dict.

181 tests pass today. A real HTML report from this run (graphtrace report, both tests, record and replay, the real Command/handoff mechanics visible in the trajectory tree) was generated and shared directly, not just described.

docs.title: Executive summary for the HTML report (2026-10-27)
docs.text:
Shown the real HTML report, the honest answer to "who reads this" was: an engineer debugging a failed test, full stop — raw Python reprs, internal jargon (subgraph_enter, node='?'), stack-trace-style error strings. Nothing in it served a QA lead, a manager, a consultant, or an auditor deciding go/no-go, even though those are exactly the roles a release-readiness report needs to serve.

Added a layer above the existing trajectory detail, not a replacement for it:

  • @pytest.mark.graphtrace(description=..., severity=..., category=...) — optional, human-authored metadata a test author attaches directly to a test. Graphtrace has no way to know on its own that "refunded without approval" is more severe than "wording changed slightly" — that's a judgment call only a human can make, and this is where it's recorded. All three default cleanly (severity to "normal", the others to None) so an untagged test still reports correctly; adopting this is additive, never required first.
  • A release verdict — READY or NOT READY, N blocking issues — computed from plain pass/fail, always meaningful regardless of whether anything was tagged.
  • Blocking issues, ranked by severity (critical first), each showing its plain-language description (or the bare test id, honestly, if none was given) and its category, linking down to the existing technical detail for whoever needs to debug it. Severity never decides whether a failure blocks — only how it's ranked and emphasized among real ones; graphtrace never gets to decide a failure is "safe to ship anyway."
  • A coverage breakdown by category — what was actually tested, not just how many things passed. Says so honestly (coverage breakdown unavailable) when nothing was tagged, rather than fabricating one from test names.
  • The existing per-test trajectory tree, judge verdicts, and raw calls are unchanged, just moved under a collapsed <details> disclosure — still there for an engineer, no longer the first (or only) thing anyone sees.

Deliberately not attempted: a trend view across multiple runs ("better or worse than last time"). That needs a separate persistence design (where history lives, how many runs to keep, per-branch or not) that wasn't designed, let alone built, here — flagged honestly rather than half-built.

examples/sample_report/ regenerated to actually demonstrate this (real descriptions/severities/categories on all three sample results, not the bare-test-id fallback). 199 tests pass today.

docs.title: Second real-world validation: langchain-ai/deepagents (2026-10-27)
docs.text:
A second real, official app — langchain-ai/deepagents (~30.6k stars, the highest-profile target researched), whose own README documents "any LangGraph CompiledStateGraph can be passed in as a sub-agent." Deliberately a different way of using a subgraph than langgraph-swarm-py's: there, "Alice"/"Bob" are direct nodes of the swarm's own compiled graph; here, the sub-agent is invoked from inside a plain tool function (task), not added as a graph node at all — different enough to surface a fourth real bug and one genuine structural limitation, neither of which the first app's testing could have.

  1. ToolRuntime (LangChain's dependency-injection object, given to a tool that declares a runtime: ToolRuntime parameter) carries the entire live Pregel execution state as its config field — per-run object ids, open file/thread handles, functools.partials. Confirmed by hand that this made the recorded cassette entry for the exact same logical call hash differently across two genuinely separate processes (default object reprs embed memory addresses), on top of bloating the cassette into something unreadable — and, found a step later while actually generating a report from it, the same raw dump was landing directly in the in-memory Trajectory itself (ToolCall.args), not just the cassette, since only the copy passed to the cassette writer had been sanitized. Fixed in both places: _yaml_safe() now recognizes ToolRuntime (lazily imported from the full langchain package, never a hard dependency) and keeps only state and tool_call_id — the only parts a human reading a cassette, or a hash matching two calls, could plausibly care about.
  2. A real, structural limitation, not a bug: a tool whose own implementation triggers a nested LangGraph execution (deepagents' task tool really does call compiled_subagent.invoke(...) inside its own Python body) loses that nested execution's own step-by-step visibility in replay mode. Confirmed by hand that record mode shows the sub-agent's own nested model step (the same subgraph_enter/exit mechanism that already handles a subgraph node), while replay mode shows only the single, opaque, cached task tool call — replaying it means the real tool body, including its own compiled_subagent.invoke(...) call, genuinely never executes. The parent's own real-world outcome (its final message) is identical either way; only the fine-grained trace of how the sub-agent itself got there is unrecoverable once that specific call is served from a cassette. Documented, not patched around — a real fix would mean recursively intercepting calls made from inside an already-intercepted call, a genuinely different and larger feature, not a quick correction.

Kept as a permanent regression test, tests/test_deepagents_compat.py (gated with pytest.importorskip, deepagents added as a second dev-extra compatibility dependency), including a real assertion for the limitation itself (record mode's trajectory has nested steps; replay mode's doesn't; both reach the identical final message) rather than leaving it as prose that could silently go stale.

201 tests pass today. A real HTML report covering both external apps was generated and shared directly.

docs.title: Real-world test depth (2026-10-27, same day)
docs.text:
Asked directly, looking at the shared report: can 3 thin, mostly happy-path tests actually justify a "READY" verdict? No — and that's exactly the overclaiming problem the executive summary work above exists to prevent, not produce. Three real additional scenarios added, using these libraries' own real test patterns again (not invented), so the coverage breakdown means something instead of showing one category once:

  • Parallel sub-agent delegation — the real pattern from deepagents' own test_multiple_subagents_invoked_in_parallel: two different sub-agents invoked concurrently from a single parent message, each completing independently with its own distinct result, confirmed not conflated or dropped.
  • A real safety property: delegating to a sub-agent type that was never registered. Confirmed the parent recovers gracefully (a normal tool result it can act on, not a crash) and that the named sub-agent's own model genuinely never ran — checked directly against the fake model's own call history, not inferred from the trajectory alone.
  • A real assert_budget check — fast and local (no real network at all) specifically so the threshold tests "did graphtrace's own interception add unreasonable overhead," not "was the network slow today."

The two langgraph-swarm-py tests were also given real categories (handoff, tool_use) they'd been missing. The report's coverage breakdown across both real apps now reads handoff, tool_use, delegation, parallel_execution, safety, performance — six distinct real dimensions, not three thin ones labeled once.

204 tests pass today.

docs.title: Real-world test depth, round two (2026-10-27, same day)
docs.text:
Asked again, more pointedly: "still only 7? can it be made of 30-50 cases?" The honest answer wasn't to pad the existing happy-path flows with reworded copies — it was to go back to both libraries' own real test suites for scenarios this project hadn't touched yet, mining deepagents' own test_file_system_tools.py, test_permissions.py, and test_todo_middleware.py, plus a few new variations built directly against the public APIs already in use (a longer swarm handoff chain, a real tool exception, extended checkpointer persistence). The real count landed at 25 real-app scenarios, not 30-50 — documented here plainly rather than padded to hit a round number that wouldn't mean anything.

tests/test_deepagents_filesystem_compat.py (new, 10 tests) — deepagents' own built-in filesystem tools (write_file, edit_file, grep, ls, delete), exercised through a full create_deep_agent() graph instead of calling backend internals directly:

  • write_file → edit_file (single replacement and replace_all), each on a real StateBackend-stored file.
  • edit_file failing gracefully on a missing file and on a missing search string — both real backend error strings, not exceptions escaping to the caller.
  • grep finding content written by two files created in parallel tool calls in a single AIMessage.
  • ls listing a freshly written file, then delete removing it — confirmed gone.
  • Four real path-traversal/safety checks (severity="high"): edit_file/read_file/write_file/ls all reject ../ traversal, a bare Windows absolute path, and a ~-prefixed path, with the real backend error string, not a crash.

One real test-authoring correction along the way, not a graphtrace bug: these tools run through LangGraph's real ToolNode, which wraps a tool's plain string return into a real ToolMessage — ToolCall.result is that ToolMessage, so assertions need .content, not a direct string comparison (already correctly handled on the serialization side; the new tests had just assumed the wrong shape at first).

tests/test_deepagents_permissions_todo_compat.py (new, 5 tests) — two more of deepagents' own real middleware features, FilesystemPermission write/delete enforcement and TodoListMiddleware, both driven through a full agent conversation instead of deepagents' own unit-level internal-function tests:

  • A write_file call denied by a FilesystemPermission(mode="deny") rule, and the identical rule set having no effect on a write outside its path (severity="high" / contrast case).
  • The real all-or-nothing recursive-delete behavior from deepagents' own TestRecursiveDeletePermissions: deleting a directory is refused whenever any file beneath it is write-denied, even if most of the subtree is unrestricted (severity="high").
  • TodoListMiddleware (not in create_deep_agent's default stack — added via its own documented middleware=[...] merge point) tracking a single write_todos call in final_state["todos"].
  • A second real structural gap, distinct from the nested-subgraph-visibility one found testing deepagents the first time: the real scenario copied from deepagents' own test_todo_middleware.py (two write_todos calls in the same AIMessage must both be rejected) revealed that TodoListMiddleware's wrap_tool_call rejection happens before graphtrace's patched BaseTool.invoke/ainvoke ever fires — traj.tool_calls is empty for both rejected calls, even though the real conversation (final_state["messages"]) carries both real error ToolMessages with the exact real error text, and todos correctly stays unset. The agent's own behavior is completely unaffected; only Trajectory.tool_calls undercounts in this one case. Documented with a real, verified assertion (assert not any(c.name == "write_todos" for c in traj.tool_calls)) rather than left as prose.

tests/test_langgraph_swarm_compat.py (3 new tests, 5 total) — three more real scenarios built directly against langgraph-swarm-py's own create_swarm/create_handoff_tool/create_agent API, verified by hand before being written:

  • A three-agent handoff chain (Alice → Bob → Carol), confirming the subgraph enter/exit fix from the first langgraph-swarm-py pass holds across more than one hop, not just the original two-agent case.
  • A real tool exception (ZeroDivisionError from a real divide tool) propagating through run_graph() with its exact real type uncorrupted — the first time this project's own documented "a live exception keeps its real type" guarantee was confirmed against a real external app's real tool error, not graphtrace's own synthetic demo agent.
  • State persisting across three conversation turns, not just two — active_agent surviving a second full handoff-and-back round trip on the same checkpointer-backed thread.

222 tests pass today. The report's coverage breakdown now spans ten real categories across two real external apps: handoff, tool_use, error_handling, state_persistence, delegation, parallel_execution, safety, performance, planning — real distinct dimensions of real library behavior, not reworded restatements of the same two flows.

docs.title: v0.2 — not started, not scheduled for v0.1
docs.text: Four pieces, all building on the already-shipped core rather than needing new infrastructure: the security test pack (scope), observability export (scope), cut-point replay (adopted from Chronicle, Microsoft, arXiv 2609.20625 — replay a recorded incident up to where it broke, then run the fix live from there), and statistical live-mode verification (adopted from AgentAssay, arXiv 2603.02601 — a Wilson-interval Pass/Fail/Inconclusive verdict across N real trials, so a single flaky nightly run stops being the whole story; see Recording & replay).

docs.title: v0.4 — not started, not scheduled for v0.1-v0.3
docs.text: CrewAI and AutoGen support (scope) — gated on v0.1 shipping first. Unlike v0.2's two features, this one required a real architecture decision made now, in v0.1: runtime/ was never built as a flat, LangGraph-only package — it's frameworks/base.py (a shared Protocol) + frameworks/langgraph/ from day one, so CrewAI/AutoGen land as new sibling packages in v0.4, not a rename of something already shipped.

docs.title: Full internal build plan
docs.text: The complete architecture — component diagrams, package layout, the cassette format, the judge contract, build order — lives in the project's own Plan/graphtrace.md (not published here; it's written for the person building graphtrace, not for the end-user guide you're reading now).

docs.title: CLI reference
docs.text: pip install -e . installs a graphtrace console command ([project.scripts] in pyproject.toml) wiring three commands — exactly what's actually built. graphtrace record and graphtrace redteam (the security test pack, v0.2) are intentionally not here yet; see Roadmap & status.

docs.title: graphtrace from-trace
docs.text:
graphtrace from-trace trace.json --target my_app.graph:build_graph [--test-name NAME] [--out PATH] [--cassette PATH]

Converts an exported trace into a cassette and a generated pytest file. See Trace-to-test for the real importer/codegen scope and the honest limits documented there.

Option Default --target (required) module:factory for the graph under test --test-name the trace file's stem --out tests/test_from_<test-name>.py --cassette tests/cassettes/from_<test-name>.yaml

docs.title: graphtrace calibrate
docs.text:
graphtrace calibrate --rubric refund_reply [--config graphtrace.yaml]

Scores the judge against graphtrace.yaml's judge.calibration_set, printing per-criterion agreement and Cohen's kappa. Exits 1 if any criterion with at least one labelled case falls below judge.min_agreement, or if graphtrace.yaml has no judge: section at all. See Judge & calibration.

docs.title: graphtrace report
docs.text:
graphtrace report results.json [--out PATH] [--title "..."] [--config graphtrace.yaml]

Renders the static HTML report from an existing results.json (written by pytest --gt-report=..., or by report/results.py's save_results() directly). --out defaults to graphtrace.yaml's report.html; --title defaults to "graphtrace report" (set it to reproduce a previous render exactly — see examples/sample_report/). See Report & CI.

docs.text:
Flag / env var Controls --gt-mode / GRAPHTRACE_MODE replay | record | record_missing | live --gt-report Write a static HTML report (+ results.json alongside it) at session end --gt-export Observability export target (v0.2, not built yet)
